f2b77097ae6198d4: PUTRAJAYA: The government has set a target for cumulative realised investment in the Northern Corridor Economic Region (NCER) to reach RM470 billion by 2030, RM126.2 billion more than the RM343.8 billion realised to date.
Key sectors including electrical and electronics (E&E), automotive, high-value tourism and modern agriculture are expected to account for 70 per cent of the targeted investment.

Northern Corridor Implementation Authority (NCIA) chief executive Datuk Mohamad Haris Kader Sultan said the region is confident of achieving the target, backed by approved investments expected to materialise over the coming years.
"We are confident that all those approved investments will be realised by 2030," he said at the launch of the NCER Strategic Development Plan 2026-2030 here today.
EV INVESTMENTS IN THE PIPELINE
As part of the push, NCER is exploring opportunities in the electric vehicle (EV) and automotive sectors to diversify its investment base beyond its established strength in E&E and semiconductors.
Mohamad Haris said several potential automotive investments are being assessed, although NCER has yet to determine how much the sector could contribute to the RM470 billion target.
"Among them are high-technology vehicle projects in Kulim, Kedah, with potential investors in the EV sector undergoing due diligence," he said.
NCER is working with the Malaysian Investment Development Authority and the Investment, Trade and Industry Ministry to assess the potential investments.
So far, two investors have been identified in the EV battery segment, while three are being considered in the automobile segment.
E&E and semiconductors will remain the mainstay of investment in the region, particularly in Penang, where about 95 per cent of investments are expected to be concentrated in the sector.
In Kedah, Kulim Hi-Tech Park remains a key investment area, while semiconductor activities are also a major attraction at Chuping Valley in Perlis.
Mohamad Haris said the diversification push is aimed at spreading economic growth beyond established investment centres and into less-developed areas across Perlis, Kedah, Penang and Perak.

Programmes and projects will be implemented in these areas to create employment opportunities, including by ensuring that sites developed with allocations from the Economy Ministry are matched with approved investments.
Mohamad Haris said approved investments typically take between two and three years to translate into actual projects, although some could take up to five years.
"The target is higher than the previous plan, but the projection was supported by investment trends, and our targets for 2020 and 2025 had been exceeded," he said.
HIGH-SKILLED JOBS IN FOCUS
Beyond investment, NCER is targeting the creation of 310,000 jobs by 2030, with 45 per cent expected to be high-skilled positions.
Mohamad Haris said the focus is not merely on increasing the number of jobs, but on attracting higher-value industries that could generate greater productivity and value-added activities.

The region is also targeting the development of 8,000 talents through the NCER Technology Innovation Centre, alongside efforts to encourage participation in technical and vocational education and training (TVET).
NCIA is working with local universities, polytechnics, TVET institutions and industry players to identify the specific disciplines and skills required by investors.
The investment and employment push is expected to help lift the region's median household income to RM7,500 by 2030.

"To achieve the new targets, NCER would coordinate cross-government, ministry and agency cooperation to link investments with talent, technology, local enterprises and supply chains, creating broader economic value," Mohamad Haris said.

Meanwhile, Economy Minister Akmal Nasrullah Mohd Nasir said the strategic plan reflects the government's commitment to translating the 13th Malaysia Plan into regional development in a structured and high-impact manner.
He said the plan would serve as a catalyst to position NCER as a leader in high-value industrial investment and a global hub for research, development, commercialisation, technology and innovation.

"These targets are not merely numbers, but a reflection of our commitment to ensuring that every ringgit of investment coming into the region is translated into higher incomes, quality jobs and greater prosperity for the people of Perlis, Kedah, Penang and Perak," he said.
Under the plan, NCER is targeting regional gross domestic product of RM369 billion by 2030, compared with RM284.8 billion currently.

Among the long-term projects expected to transform the northern region's economic landscape are the Kedah Science and Technology Park, Sidam Logistics, Advanced Manufacturing and Aerospace Hub, Kedah Rubber City, Chuping Valley Industrial Area, Bagan Datuk industrial area, Penang Silicon Island and the Northern Peninsula border economic zone.

7e4b874df4f6e383: KUALA LUMPUR, Sept 16 — The Attorney General’s Chambers (AGC) stressed that the decision not to proceed with the four charges against Tan Sri Muhyiddin Yassin in relation to Bukhary Equity Sdn Bhd was made based on a professional assessment of the evidence, the evidential viability of the case and the overall interests of the prosecution.

The AGC said the decision did not mean that the charges had been brought without basis and should not be interpreted as a finding that the transactions which were the subject of the investigation did not take place.

It said that prosecutorial decisions could and should be reviewed when the entirety of the evidence, its admissibility, the credibility of witnesses and the implications for other proceedings were assessed comprehensively, and that such decisions must be made based on the law, evidence and the interests of the administration of justice.

“The assessment showed that proceeding with the charges posed a real risk of litigation, including the risk of undermining the strategy and evidential basis of other charges still faced by the accused,” the AGC said in a statement last night.
“In such circumstances, the prosecution must consider the overall interests of the case rather than defend one charge in isolation,” it said.

The AGC also stressed that the duty of the prosecution was not to defend a particular charge at all costs, but to ensure that only charges supported by sufficient evidence and capable of being defended in court were pursued.
“After taking into account all these factors, AGC is of the view that proceeding with the charges is no longer an appropriate and prudent prosecutorial step.
“However, the prosecution involving three other predicate charges under Section 23(1) of the Malaysian Anti-Corruption Commission Act 2009 (Act 694) against the accused will continue,” it said.

High Court Judge Noor Ruwena Md Nurdin today discharged and acquitted Muhyiddin of one charge of using his position to obtain RM200 million in bribes and three money laundering charges involving the same amount after the prosecution informed the court that it would not proceed with the case against the Pagoh Member of Parliament in relation to Bukhary Equity Sdn Bhd.

Muhyiddin, 79, is now being tried on three charges of using his position to obtain RM25.3 million in bribes for Bersatu from three companies, namely Nepturis Sdn Bhd, Mamfor Sdn Bhd and KCJ Engineering Sdn Bhd, as well as Datuk Seri Azman Yusoff, in connection with the Jana Wibawa project.
The prosecution in Muhyiddin’s trial closed its case today after calling 29 prosecution witnesses. — Bernama

9da77a9fc6a4cc18: PETALING JAYA, Sept 16 — In this era where hype food like blue-coloured pasta and “bulu bulu” hairy cake pulls in diners out of curiosity and for their social media, it’s refreshing to find a humble restaurant serving good food for the neighbourhood.
MaMa Lee’s Home Cooked Kitchen definitely embodies the evergreen allure of home-style, family meals.

Opened in May, the restaurant’s awkward location in SS2 — in front of a very busy road with little parking — has led them to employ the magical words, “peng, cheng and leng,” literally translated as cheap and nice.

Strictly for weekdays, one can order a tilapia fish for RM25, compared to the usual price of RM6 per 100 grams, which would have cost me RM42. There’s a catch: you must post a Google review to qualify for the deal.
Ten different sauces are on offer, either steamed or fried, ensuring you don’t get bored if this place becomes your regular canteen.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
For those looking for a great deal, the restaurant runs a weekday dine-in promotion: RM25 for tilapia fish, provided you leave a Google review. — Picture by Lee Khang Yi
Their Lemon Thai steamed fish is a popular pick for many but I decided to try the second most ordered Nyonya curry.
The butterflied fish sits in a pool of orange curry with vegetables like eggplant, long beans and winged beans.
The flesh is smooth, especially around the belly as the fragrant curry with a little heat infuses it with flavour that calls for more rice.
We also appreciated how the vegetables were cooked to a softer consistency, probably because they prepped the curry with vegetables ahead of time.
Most restaurants don’t do this; they always throw in the vegetables at the last moment leaving them partly cooked and semi-hard. .
When you spot an entire page in the menu dedicated to yam ring with various toppings, it’s definitely a sign you must order this classic Chinese dish.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
The restaurant spans two floors and seating is a mix of round family-style tables and square tables for smaller groups. — Picture by Lee Khang Yi
Indeed the Sweet & Sour Pork Yam Ring (RM32) is a gorgeous rendition not for its looks but for the creamy texture when you start eating it.
These yam rings are prepped ahead and then fried when ordered.
A firmer bite signals a higher flour ratio, which ruins the enjoyment of this dish — the usual texture found in most places.

There is the conventional Kung Pao Chicken with its nuggets of chicken and nuts plus dried chilies, but I wanted to try the sweet and sour pork; this dish allowed me to sample both items in one order.
The pork is tender and lightly coated with batter, yielding a softer bite drenched in sauce that balances the sweet tomato sauce well with the vinegar.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Winged Bean with Lotus Root isn’t conventional and offers a fresh change from typical greens, featuring crunchiness and tender, finer beans. — Picture by Lee Khang Yi
Most restaurants treat greens as an afterthought, but once in a while, you spot a different dish like Winged Bean with Lotus Root (RM18 for small, RM28 for medium).
The four angled beans are sliced and stir fried with minced pork, aromatics like garlic and chilies, plus the unusual sliced lotus root, producing a crunchier dish than your normal plate of greens.
What makes this dish exceptional is the restaurant insists on using younger, finer beans, which aren’t woody like the older ones, providing a gentler crunch.
In general, the food here definitely reminds one of home cooking because they use salt and oil sparingly, much like how a mother cooks for her family with care.
The people behind this restaurant also operate Tien Xia Restaurant at Aurora Place, Bukit Jalil.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
As it sits next to the busy road with traffic lights, it doesn’t need much advertising. — Picture by Lee Khang Yi

7ad379dec37c5284: WASHINGTON: The US federal government is on track to approve a US$2.8 billion arms package for Israel, US media reported Tuesday, with the sale of 40,000 one-ton bombs among the largest munitions packages sold in recent years.

The Washington Post said the package – funded with US taxpayer dollars – featured some of the most destructive munitions in Western arsenals, including 20,000 MK-84s, 20,000 BLU-117s, and 20,000 I-2000 Penetrator warheads.
The New York Times said the administration of US President Donald Trump had approved the sale, citing a US official.
A senior administration official told AFP that "all foreign arms sales are moving through the appropriate process," but wouldn't comment on pending transactions.
Meanwhile, a State Department spokesperson told AFP that "as a matter of policy, the Department does not confirm or comment on proposed arms sales until they have been formally notified to Congress."

The deal was reported amid an ongoing munitions shortage within the US military, with stocks rapidly depleting from the war with Iran and with the US spending US$22.3 billion on munitions between Feb 28 and June 30.
In February 2025, the Trump administration had approved the sale of more than US$7.4 billion in bombs, missiles and related equipment to Israel, including MK-84 munitions.

In response to concerns over civilian deaths in Gaza, former US president Joe Biden's administration had blocked a shipment of 2,000-pound bombs to Israel, but the Trump administration approved them after taking office in early 2025.

b7278884c8957dfd: Many things could be done better in Malaysia, but I don’t have the energy, skill or fortitude to do them myself. Therefore, I choose to be more forgiving to those with good hearts who dive into the cesspool of politics to try to make things better.

Only those with good hearts, mind you! People who make tough choices and compromises and sacrifices but whose moral compass remains true. There aren’t many of those, so I’m not overly strained with having to accommodate them.

Recently I read some cautious statements that perhaps the affirmative action programmes which are the backbone of our national politics should be amended or phased out. However, these voices are mostly on the periphery of national politics.

Their positions are often couched in careful terms - perhaps a phased withdrawal at some uncertain date in the future or perhaps some amendments to the current programmes. Some convolute things by arguing for both “meritocracy” as well as some form of continuing affirmative action as the Malays aren’t quite ready to cut the ties to those affirmative actions yet.
False meritocracy

I’m generally not a big fan of this “meritocracy” argument. It’s often just people arguing for their own privileges, whether wealth, culture or some other forms of advantages that cement their head start, while simplistically conflating meritocracy purely through exam results and grades.

I’d rather affirmative actions be directed towards those who really need them, regardless of background. I’m myself a beneficiary of earlier affirmative actions, without which I’d probably just be a poor fisherman off Bayan Lepas staring at unemployment as the sea itself is swallowed up by artificial islands.

The original set of affirmative actions – the New Economic Policy – were actually meant to expire in 1990. That it did not wasn’t a big surprise. In 1990 many Malays were still living in remote villages far away from electricity, schools or hospitals. The aim of changing centuries of neglect within just a generation was too optimistic.

You can easily send young Malays for university education, but success in today’s capitalistic world requires a total mindset change. That transformation is difficult and carries the dangers of killing what is good about Malays – the gentle, warm and friendly folks not quite made for the dog-eat-dog world around us.
Casualties of NEP
The resulting inflamed racial politics benefited some people inordinately at the expense of the many, both Malays and non-Malays.

Another casualty is that the Malays of old, the incorruptible ones – the likes of Onn Jaafar, Dr Ismail Abdul Rahman and Ismail Ali – are mostly gone and no amount of increased piety and religiosity can replace them.

The dominant Malay mindset is one of entitlement. Behind this, however, lies something sadder: insecurity. The same insecurity made us meekly submit to four and a half centuries of colonisation and to our own feudal lords and others where fealty, often unearned, to our “betters” is expected.

Affirmative actions have helped, but also have hurt us. The crutches that helped us stand higher in the economic and other struggles unfortunately have become permanent, which we dare not contemplate living without.
Shackles of fear

Much of the claims of rights and privileges for being the original “sons of the soil” amount to just political manipulation; but they work, because of the fear among many Malays of flying untethered and competing on the same level playing fields as others.

This fear, this insecurity, hurts us. they have become institutionalised and encoded into our psyche. Privileges became rights, the temporary became permanent, regardless of what the Constitution and common sense say.

We invent new logic to support our argument. The latest came from a bunch of political ladies (some who may appear to be "constitutional" rather than ethnic Malays) who say that the old New Economic Policy goal of Malays owning 30% of the corporate wealth should now be raised to 50%, presumably as being a fairer reflection of today’s demographics.
If so, then past exhortations for Malays to reproduce aggressively so that we can “protect” the race have actually proven useful for some.
Greedy elites

Had this been an aspirational goal driving an agenda of advancement (you know, the boring stuff like smaller families, better education, stronger pride of “berdikari” – standing on our own two feet) I’d be the first to applaud it. However, this is just a pretext to carve out even more of the nation’s wealth that we couldn’t earn on our own.

This really is just about a bunch of Malay elites salivating about using politics to gain and protect easy wealth for themselves, which may result in the creation of unit trust funds meant for the bumiputera masses.

Should this happen, what will come to pass is of even more corporate wealth being owned and run by cronies and GLCs and shadowy and corrupt enablers. We’ll have even more Malay billionaires – official ones anyway – but we’ll also have more Malay families struggling to make ends meet.

We’ll never reach 50% because who wants to kill the goose that lays the golden egg? The number of Malays who struggle daily to put food on the table of their large families will remain high because they’re a convenient excuse for politicians.

More non-Malays will feel disenfranchised. Many Malays – those who have options elsewhere – will also be disheartened. Then one day we may even demand 100% of the corporate pie for Malays because Malaysia has lost all non-Malays even while the economic pie itself has shrunk to a measly cookie.
Take off the crutches

When we celebrate national independence -- which no West Malaysian alive (except for perhaps one) had actually fought for -- we talk about being independent of colonisers, we don’t talk enough about being independent in our own mind. We’re still haunted by fears of others not like us and easily kept in line by our own who are supposedly “better” than us.
And so here we are, not just politically independent but a nation that’s an even more complex and volatile mix.

It's about time we accept that not everything is about us and that we’re actually tougher than we think – if only we dare to put ourselves to the test. Enough with this rubbish about extending affirmative action. They helped to make us stronger, but now they are making us weaker. We’re now more addicted, more frightened and more angry when we think about living without the privileges.

Let’s have a different kind of conversation. Let’s accept that true independence is being able to stand on our two feet and being able to help others instead of asking help for ourselves. For Malaysia to succeed, we Malays must feel confident we can happily and independently co-exist with fellow Malaysians without worrying about our survival.
With that, Happy Malaysia Day to one and all Malaysians.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.
da44aa6d2588598e: KUALA LUMPUR: Two Port Dickson-based refiners are seeing sharply diverging fortunes on Bursa Malaysia, with Hengyuan Refining Co Bhd outperforming Petron Malaysia Refining & Marketing Bhd as investors weigh their ability to benefit from elevated refining margins.
Hengyuan's shares have surged more than fourfold this year, with the refiner emerging as a major outperformer amid heightened US-Iran tensions.
The stock has jumped 353 per cent to RM3.49 from 77 sen on Jan 2 so far this year. From end of February, when the US-Iran conflict began, Hengyuan's share price has rallied by more than 250 per cent.
Since both companies reported their second-quarter (Q2) results on Aug 28, Hengyuan's share price has surged about 77 per cent to RM3.45 as at Sept 14, from RM1.95.
The rally accelerated alongside the renewed escalation in the US-Iran conflict on Sept 1.
Petron, meanwhile, saw its shares edge up only about 5.7 per cent to RM3.53 from RM3.34 over the same period.
The share price also has fallen about 9.0 per cent year to date from RM3.88 at the start of the year.
The stock initially gained during the February escalation, rising 10.6 per cent from RM4.15 to RM4.59.
It subsequently reached a 2026 peak of RM4.90 before retreating 31.8 per cent to RM3.34, although it has since recovered to RM3.53.
Petron's market capitalisation stood at about RM953 million.
The divergent share-price performance means Hengyuan has added roughly RM1.6 billion to its market value since the start of the year, while Petron's market value remains below RM1 billion.

Tradeview Capital fund manager Neoh Jia Man said the divergence comes as Hengyuan is able to capture the improving refining economics, while Petron Malaysia's operation continues to face disruptions following the collapse of its product jetty at its Port Dickson refinery last year.
"As a result, Petron is unable to fully capture the upside from the higher refining margins.
"In addition, unlike Hengyuan, Petron Malaysia has sizable fuel retail and commercial supply businesses, which dilute its overall exposure to the refining sector," he told the Business Times.

With the new jetty only targeted for commissioning in the first quarter (Q1) of 2027, Neoh said Petron's refinery operations remain constrained in the interim, requiring the company to rely primarily on imported refined products.
This limits its ability to fully benefit from the current refining-margin upcycle compared with Hengyuan, he said.
The diverging fortunes of the two listed oil refineries on Bursa Malaysia can also be seen through their financial results over the last two quarters.
In the first quarter ended March 31, 2026, Hengyuan staged a remarkable turnaround, chalking a net profit of RM525.55 million, from a net loss of RM170.45 million in the corresponding quarter.

Its net profits continued to increase in the second quarter ended June 30, 2026, at RM600.54 million, a 14.3 per cent increase quarter-on-quarter. In the first half of the year, Hengyuan's net profits exceeded RM1.13 billion, compared with a net loss of RM353.7 million a year ago.

On the other hand, Petron Malaysia suffered a net loss of RM35.04 million in Q1 FY26, as production halted during the quarter due to the destruction of its product jetty following tropical storm Senyar in November 2025.
The group continues to chalk a net loss of RM34.5 million during Q2 FY26.
REFINERIES ENJOYING ELEVATED CRACK SPREADS

Crude oil refineries have been enjoying elevated crack spreads – the price difference between a barrel of crude oil and the average output of refined product – since the outbreak of the US-Iran war starting Feb 2026.
According to data compiled by Trading Economics, the crack spread index of US refineries stood at 62.36 points as of Sept 15, near the multi-year high of 70 points reached early this month.
While the spread has fallen 10.06 per cent over the past month, it is still 136.85 per cent higher than a year ago.
Neoh noted that Hengyuan is positioned to capture any further improvement in crack spreads, with the company having no major refinery turnaround scheduled until 2028.
Based on Tradeview Capital's estimates, he said Singapore's complex refining margin had moderated substantially in September but remained at an elevated level.
"We believe Hengyuan is well positioned to capture any further widening in crack spreads, given that it has no major refinery turnaround scheduled until 2028.

"Furthermore, only around 20 per cent of its crude supply is sourced from the Middle East, limiting its exposure to potential supply disruptions arising from the current geopolitical instability in the region," it said.
HOW MUCH LONGER WILL AN ELEVATED MARGIN STAY?

The conflict in the Middle East continues to disrupt the global oil trade as flow of the liquid through the Strait of Hormuz is interrupted, as both the US and Iran are unable to come to an agreement of a cease fire.

Iran's attack on Saudi Arabia's oil facilities, including the huge east-west oil pipeline, threatens loss of 4% of global oil supply. Meanwhile, the Islamic Republic's proxy – the Houthis in Yemen – have seized control of the Bab al-Mandeb strait – the only route to access the Suez Canal.
However, BIMB Securities Research noted that this escalatory cycle is unlikely to be sustained, due to logistics limitations for the US.
"Our bullish tilt on oil prices (US$110 to US$120 highs) is likely to reverse within a two to four week window, based on the previous patterns," said the research firm in a note on Sept 15.

The research firm reiterates its trading tilts on Hibiscus Petroleum Bhd, which is a direct proxy to oil prices, Petronas Chemicals Group Bhd (benefitting from the higher fertilizer prices) and Hengyuan. The firm does not cover Hengyuan.
"Of the three, we see Hengyuan having the most room to surprise on the upside, including earnings, thanks to its exposure to the crack spreads.
"However, as highlighted earlier, we remain mindful that the current surge in oil prices is unlikely to persist – and likewise the catalyst for the stocks," the research firm noted.
It said that Hengyuan's windfall profit of RM1.1 billion in 1H FY26, which translates into an earnings per share of RM1.78, when annualised could reach around RM3.60 per share.

"Despite the 358 per cent YTD share price rally, this would still imply a price-earnings multiple of only around one time, suggesting that valuation remains undemanding relative to the prevailing earnings run rate.
"In our view, the key question is therefore not how far Hengyuan's share price has risen, but how long the current elevated crack spread environment can persist," the research firm said.

7e3302294293e6be: KUALA LUMPUR: Australia is becoming an increasingly important growth engine for Malaysian companies, as they tap billions of ringgit worth of opportunities spanning infrastructure, renewable energy (RE), mining and property.

The scale of that exposure is already significant for some Bursa Malaysia-listed firms such as Gamuda Bhd, which boasts more than one-third of its RM61.6 billion outstanding order book tied to Australian construction jobs.

CIMB Securities Sdn Bhd analysts Kenny Mak Hoy Ken and Wei Yi Tan said Australia's appeal as an investment destination is backed by favourable migration trends, opportunities for scalable operations and a sound business environment.
"The core investment focus of Malaysian corporates and government-backed entities in Australia is centred on the four sectors which continue to provide long-term value," they said in a note.

Infrastructure is among the areas where the scale of opportunity is particularly pronounced, with major spending programmes across several Australian states opening up potential work for Malaysian firms.

For Sime Darby Bhd's industrial arm, the opportunities include RM21 billion of spending ahead of the 2032 Brisbane Olympics, Sydney Metro's RM60 billion investment plan over the next four years and Western Australia's aim to attract RM160 billion in private investments over four years.
Gamuda, meanwhile, has established itself as one of Australia's leading Tier-1 contractors since entering the market in 2015, the analysts said.
Its Australian operations now employ about 2,500 people and span major rail, road and RE projects.
The company is currently undertaking the RM7.3 billion Sydney Metro West Stations Package West after winding down work on the RM6.5 billion Western Tunnelling Package.
It recently added the RM2.5 billion Parramatta Integrated Station Development, its third major Sydney Metro contract, in which Gamuda has an effective 80 per cent participation.
The latest win means Gamuda has secured six of the nine station packages along the Sydney Metro West line.

CIMB Securities expects the Parramatta station works to potentially generate pre-tax margins of up to eight per cent, compared with the typical five to six per cent for its conventional Australian infrastructure jobs.
The group is also part of a consortium shortlisted for a construction package under the Sydney-Newcastle high-speed rail project, whose overall cost is projected at up to AU$90 billion.
Australia's energy transition is opening another avenue for Malaysian capital.
The country is targeting RE to account for 82 per cent of electricity generation by 2030, requiring further private investment in generation, storage and transmission infrastructure.
Investment in utility-scale solar alone reached a record AU$3 billion in the first half of 2026, compared with AU$876 million in the second half of last year.
CIMB Securities said discussions with Malaysian infrastructure and utility players operating there pointed to an upbeat longer-term view of Australia's clean-energy transition.
"Leading the Malaysian charge in Australia's booming RE market are Gamuda and Petroliam Nasional Bhd (Petronas)-backed Gentari Australia," it said.
Gamuda has already secured projects across solar, wind, hydro, battery storage and electricity transmission, while increasingly moving beyond construction into ownership of RE assets.
The company has raised its target for RE assets under development, construction and operation to five gigawatts (GW) by 2031.
This is after achieving its initial target of building a 1GW to 2GW portfolio by 2029, within two years of entering Australia's energy market.
Australian projects are expected to make up a substantial portion of the enlarged portfolio.
Petronas' Gentari is also building its Australian footprint.

Its RE portfolio currently comprises 422 megawatts (MW) of installed capacity, with another 571MW under management. Its flagship Maryvale project in New South Wales pairs a 243MW-peak solar farm with a 172MW battery energy storage system.
Property is emerging as another area of Malaysian interest, although developers are becoming more selective as Australia's broader residential market softens.
CIMB Securities said Malaysian developers were increasingly targeting purpose-built student accommodation, co-living and rental housing, particularly in Melbourne and Sydney.

"The Malaysian developers are focusing on the more resilient living sub-sectors such as purpose-built student accommodation as well as co-living accommodation schemes that offer flexible, community-focused living with shared amenities," it said.

The opportunity is driven by a shortage of student accommodation. Cushman & Wakefield estimates Melbourne alone could face a shortfall of as many as 200,000 student housing beds, based on 2023 enrolment levels.
Malaysian developers with projects or expansion plans in Australia include SP Setia Bhd, Sime Darby Property Bhd, UEM Sunrise Bhd, Matrix Concepts Holdings Bhd, MRCB and Gamuda.
For CIMB Securities, Gamuda remains its preferred Malaysian stock for exposure to Australia's infrastructure and RE pipeline.
The research firm said the size of Gamuda's Australian order book underscored the country's growing importance to the group.

It said the RM61.6 billion record order book, of which Australian construction jobs account for 35 per cent, highlighted "Australia's strategic importance in sustaining Gamuda's order book replenishment trajectory.

d7c0e102ece23b51: WASHINGTON: US President Donald Trump threatened Tuesday to keep the Kennedy Center closed for good after a judge ruled his name cannot be added onto the famed arts institution's facade.
Trump said his hand-picked board voted "almost unanimously" to shut the venue immediately for emergency renovations, just a few hours after the federal judge's decision.
But he warned the "very large and complex" repairs at the building in Washington cannot begin until a higher court rules on whether the center can be renamed after himself.

"If the ruling is a negative one, which it should not be, and is not overturned by the US Supreme Court, the Reconstruction and the Renovation of The Kennedy Center will not take place," Trump said on his Truth Social network.
The Kennedy Center said in a statement to AFP that the board's decision "reflects sound judgment and a clear prioritization of safety above all else."

Shortly after beginning his second term, Republican Trump installed himself as chairman of the center, which is named in honour of late president John F. Kennedy, a Democrat who championed civil rights before he was assassinated in 1963.
The board voted in December to call it the "Trump-Kennedy" Center and installed signage with his name on it.
US federal judge Christopher Cooper previously ordered Trump's name removed from the exterior and overturned the board's decision to rename the institution.
Cooper ruled on Tuesday that Trump's name cannot be added back, rebuking the center for trying to circumvent his earlier order.
"Simply put," wrote Cooper in his decision, the board "cannot install memorials for President Trump or anyone or anything else at the Kennedy Center without Congress's blessing."
Trump himself called into the board meeting and berated a Democratic congresswoman who serves on the board and filed the lawsuit that blocked its renaming, CNN reported.
The Kennedy Center takeover is one of several projects aimed at stamping Trump's brand on the US capital, including a triumphal arch and a half-billion dollar ballroom at the White House.
Workers removed Trump's name from the building in June, but scaffolding and tarps have remained ever since.
Last month, the board moved forward with a plan to add a new signage on the building that would read "renovated and restored by President Donald J. Trump."
Cooper on Tuesday said that plan was in violation of his previous ruling.
Trump and his chosen leaders of the Kennedy Center have argued that its main building, which was constructed in the 1960s, is in a state of dangerous disrepair.
As evidence of the safety problems, the president pointed to a recent incident in which a piece of the ceiling tumbled to the ground following a storm.
"If the Building were open, innocent people would have been killed," he wrote in a post on Truth Social before the judge's ruling.
Last month, as part of court proceedings, the Trump administration warned that the center may need to be demolished, if its plans to renovate the building were blocked.
A host of artists canceled concerts at the venue in response to Trump's takeover, while US media has reported that Kennedy Center ticket sales have plummeted.
38dec8f4e275400e: LIVERPOOL: Roberto De Zerbi admitted Tottenham are in a "tough moment" as he apologised for their League Cup exit in a dismal 3-1 defeat against Liverpool on Tuesday.
After a woeful start to the Premier League season, Tottenham's hopes of a morale-boosting cup run came to a dispiriting end at rain-lashed Anfield.
They were swatted aside by Liverpool, with Alexis Mac Allister, Cody Gakpo and Dominik Szoboszlai scoring for the Reds.
Conor Gallagher's reply, which came with Tottenham trailing 2-0, was their first goal against top-flight opponents this term.
De Zerbi's fourth-bottom team are without a win in their first four league matches, losing twice and drawing twice.
De Zerbi claimed Tottenham have been unlucky this season.
"We have to shoot more times, we have to shoot better, but we are sorry for the result, disappointed, frustrated for the result," he said.
"I think, unfair, but we have to accept and to be stronger than this unlucky moment.
"I'm honest with myself and I'm honest with you. I think in these five, six games, we have been for sure not lucky with Newcastle, with Everton, even with Nottingham and tonight as well."
Tottenham's only win this season has come in the League Cup against second-tier Charlton.

After successive 17th place finishes – including avoiding relegation on the final day of last season – the north London club spent over £300 million ($404 million) on 10 new signings since the end of last term.
Making eight changes from last weekend's draw with Everton was a gamble that backfired for De Zerbi as his side were beaten by an under-strength Liverpool line-up.
But former Marseille boss De Zerbi, whose appointment late last season saved Tottenham from relegation, is convinced they are still on the right path.
"We have to understand if we are in the right way or not," he said.
"I think watching the game, the last three games, four games, maybe until minute 60 with Newcastle, I think we are in the right way.
"I believe in my players, I have a big confidence, a big opinion of my players, and when we arrive to find the click, to win a game.
"I think we enjoy with these players, because the qualities of the players are incredible."
Accepting the blame for Tottenham's woeful start to the season, De Zerbi vowed they will bounce back at home to Aston Villa on Saturday.
"I'm sorry, and it's my responsibility. Because maybe in the middle of the first half we didn't recognise the clear situation man-to-man," he said.

5476bed8f4f838c3: KUALA LUMPUR: Going solo has emerged as Pakatan Harapan's most strategic option for the upcoming Melaka state polls as cooperation with Barisan Nasional has reached an impasse, political analysts said.
This follows BN's firm stance to defend all 21 seats it won in the 2021 state election.
The issue escalated after acting Melaka PKR chief Adam Adli Abd Halim said PH was ready to contest all 28 state seats independently.
Ilham Centre executive director Hisommudin Bakar said the lack of progress in seat allocation left PH with no choice but to build its own electoral narrative ahead of the polls.
"Adam's statement is a clear signal that PH cannot afford to wait indefinitely for BN.

"PH must prepare its supporters early for the reality that political cooperation in Putrajaya will not automatically translate into a formal electoral alliance at the state level," he told the New Straits Times.

Hisommudin said, with BN holding a solid two-thirds majority, PH's primary focus must shift towards safeguarding its five incumbent seats held by DAP and Amanah, while strategically targeting a handful of mixed battlegrounds to preserve its regional influence.
On Sunday, Adam said the party had to be prepared for the polls, adding that it was not as if PH had never contested all seats before.
"We must always be prepared because whether to negotiate or not is a choice, and every party has the right to decide.
"Contesting all seats will not be an issue for us."

Universiti Malaya political analyst Dr Mohammad Tawfik Yaakub said Adam's declaration was both a practical contingency plan and a calculated negotiating posture intended to pressure BN leadership into commencing formal talks on equitable terms.
"PH's strongest claim is for seats it currently holds or where it maintains a proven competitive record, particularly in urban and mixed constituencies."

He said deferring talks until after the state legislative assembly is officially dissolved would put PH at a severe disadvantage, potentially sparking sabotage and candidate friction due to a compressed campaign timeline.
He added that going solo presented a formidable challenge for PH, given the state's current political makeup.

Universiti Teknologi Malaysia Faculty of Social Sciences and Humanities' Associate Professor Dr Mazlan Ali said that current political indicators suggested that BN would rely on its established machinery, likely restricting PH's wins to between five and seven seats within Chinese-majority and urban mixed areas.

He said that while DAP retained a firm footing in its traditional strongholds, PKR faced a tougher battle to reclaim lost territory unless it successfully capitalises on urban middle-class sentiment over national issues.

"Current indicators suggest that BN could retain the number of seats it previously won. Although PH may not take over Melaka from BN, PH still stands a chance of winning at least seven state assembly seats in Chinese-majority and urban mixed constituencies.
"It might be more difficult for PKR to win seats compared with DAP."
The analysts also said that a direct contest between PH and BN in Melaka would not threaten the stability of the unity government led by Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim

95111bbc82fce2a5: Malaysian football has seen plenty of new beginnings.
This one comes with a particularly familiar cast.

The Football Association of Malaysia (FAM) goes to the polls tomorrow to elect a president and a new executive committee, seven months after its entire 17-member leadership stepped down following an AFC governance review.
The statutes have been rewritten, the executive committee cut to 11 members, clubs given a greater formal voice and eligibility rules tightened.
On paper, the machinery looks different.
Then comes the candidate list.

Of the 28 candidates whose eligibility and intention to contest have been confirmed, 17 have established FAM connections, including 12 who served on the executive committee that resigned en masse in January.
Only 11 are newcomers who have never sat on FAM’s executive board.
That sits uneasily with an election being presented as the start of a new era.
So why should anyone believe FAM will really change when so much of the old FAM is still seeking a seat at the table?
FAM’s credibility was damaged by a governance failure. Its response was to replace the leadership, submit to an external review and rewrite the rules.
Now a significant proportion of the people from that previous administration are seeking office again.
So what, precisely, is the election supposed to demonstrate?
The answer cannot simply be that the rules have changed.
Rules matter, but rules do not govern football. People do.
That makes this election more than a contest between Ab Ghani Hassan and Shahril Mokhtar for the presidency.
Both come with administrative credentials. Ghani heads the Malaysian Football League, while Shahril is deputy president of the Football Association of Selangor.
Their supporters can make the case for their experience, programmes and ability to lead.
But whoever wins inherits a problem much larger than the presidency.
FAM needs credibility.
That became painfully clear last year when Fifa sanctioned FAM over falsified documentation used in the registration of seven foreign-born players.
Fifa fined the association about RM1.9 million and banned the players for 12 months. The Court of Arbitration for Sport later upheld the disciplinary consequences.
The finding went beyond an administrative lapse. Fifa said using fraudulent documentation to make a player eligible to compete amounted to cheating and damaged trust in the fairness of football.
That trust is now central to Malaysian football’s recovery.
Changing the furniture will not restore it.

The January mass resignation was supposed to mark a decisive break. FAM said the executive committee’s departure would protect the association’s integrity and reputation, allow investigations and internal processes to proceed without interference, and help restore public confidence.
Those were serious words.
Seven months later, some of the same people are seeking office again.
There is nothing inherently improper about an experienced administrator standing for election.
Previous service should not become a lifetime ban from public office. Nor should every former office-bearer carry personal responsibility for every failure during a collective tenure.
But an organisation emerging from a governance crisis cannot expect the public to ignore the symbolism.
If the mass resignation was part of the process of rebuilding confidence, what does it say when much of the same political ecosystem reappears at the next election?
This is not about personalities but about institutional memory.
For months, FAM has responded to pressure from outside, first with Fifa sanctions, then an AFC governance review and finally a rewrite of its statutes shaped by the continental body.
Now the association has to show that it can govern differently without waiting for another crisis, another audit or another international intervention to tell it what needs fixing.

The new statutes give FAM useful tools. A smaller executive committee should make responsibility clearer. Greater representation for professional clubs could broaden decision-making. Tighter eligibility rules should raise the standard for those seeking office.
But no statute can guarantee good governance.
A carefully rewritten rulebook can still sit in the hands of people comfortable with old habits.
That is why the composition of the new executive committee matters as much as the identity of the president.

Will members challenge decisions when they should? Will they insist on proper documentation? Will they accept scrutiny? Will they put the association’s interests ahead of personal, state or club loyalties?
And will anyone tell a powerful colleague when something is wrong?
The public, meanwhile, is not obliged to regard Sept 17 as a cure.
For many supporters, this will be another event inside a football administration that has spent too long asking for patience.

The national team continues to deal with the fallout from the naturalisation scandal, Fifa’s sanctions remain in force and Malaysian football is still trying to repair a reputation damaged far beyond its own borders.
A new president cannot erase that with a victory speech.
Nor can a new executive committee demand confidence simply because affiliates have elected it.
Confidence will return only when FAM makes decisions that withstand scrutiny and accepts accountability when things go wrong.
That means looking beyond the campaign.
The real measure will be whether the new leadership strengthens internal controls, demands proper governance and gives newcomers room to challenge established thinking.
It will also be whether returning administrators recognise that experience has value only when it comes with the willingness to confront what went wrong.
An election can change who occupies the room without changing what happens inside it. That is why the return of so many familiar figures deserves scrutiny.

After everything Malaysian football has been through, FAM is asking the public to believe that a new structure will deliver a different culture while many of the people from the old structure are asking for another turn at running it.
The question is no longer whether FAM can announce a new beginning. It is whether anyone outside the room has enough reason to believe it.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.
a8634853e962823e: Bola sepak Malaysia sudah berkali-kali menyaksikan permulaan baharu.
Namun kali ini, ramai watak yang muncul masih kelihatan begitu dikenali.

Persatuan Bolasepak Malaysia (FAM) akan mengadakan pemilihan esok bagi memilih presiden serta barisan jawatankuasa eksekutif baharu, tujuh bulan selepas kesemua 17 anggota kepimpinannya meletakkan jawatan susulan semakan tadbir urus oleh Konfederasi Bolasepak Asia (AFC).
Peraturan FAM sudah disemak semula, jumlah anggota jawatankuasa eksekutif dikurangkan kepada 11 orang, kelab diberi peranan lebih besar secara rasmi, manakala syarat kelayakan calon diperketatkan.
Di atas kertas, struktur pentadbirannya kelihatan berbeza. Namun, senarai calon memberi gambaran lain.

Daripada 28 calon yang disahkan layak dan berhasrat bertanding, 17 mempunyai kaitan lama dengan FAM, termasuk 12 individu yang pernah menganggotai jawatankuasa eksekutif yang meletakkan jawatan secara beramai-ramai pada Januari.
Hanya 11 calon benar-benar muka baharu yang tidak pernah menganggotai barisan eksekutif FAM.
Keadaan itu sukar diselaraskan dengan gambaran bahawa pemilihan ini akan membuka lembaran baharu.
Jadi, mengapa orang ramai harus percaya FAM benar-benar akan berubah apabila begitu ramai daripada kelompok lama masih mahu kembali mendapat tempat dalam kepimpinan?
Kredibiliti FAM terjejas akibat kegagalan tadbir urus. Sebagai tindak balas, kepimpinannya berundur, badan itu menjalani semakan luar dan peraturannya ditulis semula.
Kini, sebahagian besar individu daripada pentadbiran terdahulu mahu kembali memegang jawatan.
Jadi, apakah sebenarnya yang mahu dibuktikan menerusi pemilihan ini?
Jawapannya tidak boleh sekadar bahawa peraturannya sudah berubah.
Peraturan memang penting, tetapi bukan peraturan yang mentadbir bola sepak. Manusialah yang melaksanakannya.
Sebab itu, pemilihan ini bukan sekadar persaingan antara Ab Ghani Hassan dan Shahril Mokhtar bagi merebut jawatan presiden.
Kedua-duanya mempunyai pengalaman pentadbiran. Ghani mengetuai Liga Bolasepak Malaysia (MFL), manakala Shahril ialah timbalan presiden Persatuan Bolasepak Selangor.
Penyokong masing-masing boleh mengetengahkan pengalaman, program dan keupayaan mereka untuk memimpin.
Namun, siapa pun yang menang akan mewarisi masalah yang jauh lebih besar daripada soal jawatan presiden.
FAM perlu memulihkan kredibilitinya.
Keperluan itu menjadi semakin jelas tahun lalu apabila Fifa mengenakan tindakan terhadap FAM berhubung penggunaan dokumen palsu dalam pendaftaran tujuh pemain kelahiran luar negara.
Fifa mendenda persatuan itu kira-kira RM1.9 juta dan menggantung pemain terbabit selama 12 bulan. Mahkamah Timbang Tara Sukan (CAS) kemudian mengekalkan tindakan disiplin berkenaan.

Kesalahan itu bukan sekadar kecuaian pentadbiran. Fifa menyatakan penggunaan dokumen palsu bagi melayakkan seseorang pemain bertanding merupakan satu bentuk penipuan dan menjejaskan keyakinan terhadap keadilan dalam bola sepak.
Kepercayaan itulah yang kini perlu dipulihkan oleh bola sepak Malaysia.
Sekadar menukar orang dan susunan organisasi tidak akan mengembalikannya.

Peletakan jawatan beramai-ramai pada Januari sepatutnya menjadi titik perubahan yang jelas. FAM ketika itu menyatakan pengunduran jawatankuasa eksekutif bertujuan melindungi integriti dan reputasi persatuan, membolehkan siasatan serta proses dalaman berjalan tanpa gangguan dan membantu mengembalikan keyakinan orang ramai.
Itu bukan kenyataan yang kecil maknanya.
Namun tujuh bulan kemudian, sebahagian individu sama mahu kembali memegang jawatan.
Tidak ada salahnya seseorang pentadbir berpengalaman bertanding semula.

Pengalaman berkhidmat sebelum ini tidak sepatutnya menjadi alasan untuk menghalang seseorang daripada memegang jawatan selama-lamanya. Begitu juga, tidak semua bekas pemegang jawatan boleh dipertanggungjawabkan secara peribadi atas setiap kegagalan yang berlaku ketika mereka menjadi sebahagian daripada sesuatu pentadbiran.
Tetapi sebuah organisasi yang baru keluar daripada krisis tadbir urus tidak boleh mengharapkan orang ramai mengabaikan apa yang tersirat.

Jika peletakan jawatan beramai-ramai itu sebahagian daripada usaha membina semula keyakinan, apakah mesej yang dihantar apabila kelompok politik dan pentadbiran sama kembali muncul dalam pemilihan berikutnya?
Ini bukan soal individu, tetapi soal budaya dan ingatan institusi.

Selama berbulan-bulan, FAM bertindak balas terhadap tekanan dari luar — bermula dengan sekatan Fifa, diikuti semakan tadbir urus AFC dan akhirnya penulisan semula statut yang dipengaruhi badan bola sepak benua itu.
Kini FAM perlu membuktikan bahawa ia mampu menguruskan dirinya secara berbeza tanpa perlu menunggu satu lagi krisis, audit atau campur tangan antarabangsa untuk memberitahu apa yang perlu diperbaiki.

Statut baharu memberi FAM beberapa mekanisme berguna. Jawatankuasa eksekutif yang lebih kecil sepatutnya memperjelas tanggungjawab. Penyertaan lebih besar daripada kelab profesional boleh meluaskan proses membuat keputusan. Syarat kelayakan yang lebih ketat pula sepatutnya meningkatkan standard mereka yang mahu memegang jawatan.
Namun, tiada statut yang mampu menjamin tadbir urus yang baik.
Peraturan yang ditulis dengan teliti masih boleh berada di tangan individu yang selesa dengan cara lama.
Sebab itu, komposisi jawatankuasa eksekutif baharu sama penting dengan siapa yang dipilih menjadi presiden.

Adakah anggotanya sanggup mempersoalkan sesuatu keputusan apabila perlu? Adakah mereka akan memastikan semua dokumentasi dibuat dengan betul? Adakah mereka bersedia menerima penelitian? Adakah mereka akan mendahulukan kepentingan persatuan berbanding kepentingan peribadi, negeri atau kelab?
Dan adakah sesiapa berani menegur rakan yang berpengaruh apabila sesuatu perkara tidak kena?
Orang ramai pula tidak wajib menganggap 17 Sept sebagai penyelesaian kepada segala masalah.
Bagi ramai penyokong, pemilihan ini mungkin hanya satu lagi episod dalam pentadbiran bola sepak yang sudah terlalu lama meminta mereka bersabar.

Pasukan kebangsaan masih berdepan kesan daripada skandal naturalisasi, sekatan Fifa masih berkuat kuasa dan bola sepak Malaysia masih berusaha memulihkan reputasi yang tercalar jauh melangkaui sempadan negara.
Presiden baharu tidak mampu memadam semua itu hanya dengan ucapan kemenangan.
Begitu juga, jawatankuasa eksekutif baharu tidak boleh mengharapkan keyakinan orang ramai hanya kerana mereka dipilih oleh ahli gabungan.
Keyakinan hanya akan kembali apabila FAM membuat keputusan yang mampu bertahan apabila diperiksa dan bersedia menerima tanggungjawab apabila berlaku kesilapan.
Sebab itu, perhatian tidak seharusnya terhenti pada pemilihan semata-mata.
Ukuran sebenar ialah sama ada kepimpinan baharu akan memperkukuh kawalan dalaman, menegakkan tadbir urus yang betul dan memberi ruang kepada muka baharu untuk mencabar cara pemikiran lama.
Ia juga bergantung kepada sama ada pentadbir lama yang kembali memahami bahawa pengalaman hanya bernilai jika disertai kesediaan mengakui dan menangani apa yang pernah berlaku.

Sesuatu pemilihan boleh menukar individu yang berada dalam bilik, tetapi belum tentu mengubah apa yang berlaku di dalamnya. Sebab itu, kemunculan semula begitu ramai wajah lama wajar diperhatikan dengan teliti.

Selepas segala yang dilalui bola sepak Malaysia, FAM kini meminta orang ramai percaya bahawa struktur baharu akan melahirkan budaya berbeza, sedangkan ramai daripada mereka yang berada dalam struktur lama kembali meminta peluang untuk mentadbirnya.
Persoalannya kini bukan lagi sama ada FAM mampu mengumumkan satu permulaan baharu.
Persoalannya ialah sama ada orang di luar lingkungan FAM mempunyai alasan yang cukup untuk mempercayainya.
Artikel ini adalah pandangan penulis dan tidak semestinya mewakili FMT.
4a2e7915a7a18488: WASHINGTON: US Attorney General Todd Blanche said on Tuesday the FBI had discovered new information regarding the shooter who attempted to assassinate Donald Trump during a campaign event in Butler, Pennsylvania, in 2024.

"It is new information about the shooter and about his background, about his history and that stuff that we didn't know before," Blanche told reporters during a White House press conference, declining to elaborate.

A person who reviewed documents detailing the new information said it includes that the shooter had packages delivered to him under the pseudonym Bob Dole, the late Republican senator and presidential candidate.
The records also note that the shooter purchased parts and tools to increase his rifle's capacity from Amazon, the person said, who declined to be identified because the documents are not public.

An anonymous donor also paid to cremate the remains of the shooter, who was killed by a Secret Service sniper during the assassination attempt, which came as a total surprise to the family, according to the documents the person reviewed.

The gunman fired eight shots before he was killed, including one that grazed Trump's ear and one that killed a bystander and injured two others. Investigators still have not identified a motive, the person added.

The comments from Blanche came hours after Trump claimed on social media that new information was found about the assassination attempt and alleged without evidence that it was really a "Democrat Plot, to get me out of the Election."
Investigations into the shooting have found the shooter acted alone and produced no evidence Democrats had anything to do with the shooting.

Trump added that former FBI Director Christopher Wray, whom Trump appointed in his first term but later grew to hate, "should pay a price" for how the department responded to the assassination attempt "and certainly for the things he said."

Blanche, who was Trump's personal lawyer at the time of the assassination attempt, said during the briefing that he was with Trump as the investigation into the shooting was playing out, trying to ascertain what happened.
"His frustration and concern about what the former director was doing is something that is not new," Blanche said.
The Justice Department and FBI did not immediately respond to requests for comment, and the White House referred to Blanche's comments. Wray could not be reached for comment.

f4d883f604bc77c3: KUALA LUMPUR: The armed forces are sharpening a strategy for the future with a five-pronged approach — from diplomacy and detecting threats early to deterring, denying and, if necessary, defeating them.

Armed Forces chief General Tan Sri Malek Razak Sulaiman said the strategy was aimed at ensuring the force remained credible and prepared to deal with threats across the land, sea, air, cyber and electromagnetic domains.

He said this year's 93rd Armed Forces Day theme, "Armed Forces' Resilience, the Nation's Defence Bastion" (Ketahanan ATM, Benteng Pertahanan Negara), reflected the importance of resilience in enabling the force to fulfil its core responsibility of safeguarding national security and sovereignty.
"Resilience is important because it determines whether the armed forces can fulfil the main duty of safeguarding the security and sovereignty of the country.
"Without resilience, trust in our ability to carry out that task may be weakened.

"Resilience is not limited to physical strength or military assets, but is built on three values under the 'ATM' approach – Akhlak Teras (Core Character), Tatakelola Tuntas (Comprehensive Governance) and Martabat Tempur (Combat Readiness)."
He said Akhlak Teras formed the foundation through the strength of character among personnel and formations.
Tatakelola Tuntas covered the management of people, assets, procurement and finances, with integrity, honesty, sincerity and trust at its core.
"After we have strong character and good governance, we have Martabat Tempur.
"This supports our mission to safeguard security and sovereignty and gives our stakeholders the assurance that we are ready to carry out our responsibilities."
THE 5D STRATEGY
Malek said the 5D strategy — Diplomacy, Detect, Deter, Deny and Defeat — provided the strategic approach for developing a credible "Future Force".

He said Diplomacy involved using diplomatic channels to reduce risks before resorting to other measures, while Detect focused on building the knowledge and early-warning capability needed to identify potential threats.
"Diplomacy is important because before we take physical action, we must first reduce the risk through diplomatic channels.
"Then, through Detect, we must know and understand the threat before it arrives or builds up its strength.
"The Detect component requires stronger detection, communications and intelligence systems, while Deter is aimed at imposing costs on potential threats and preventing them from escalating."
He said such costs could involve time, space, assets and sustainment, creating sufficient deterrence for anyone with hostile intent against Malaysia.
"When we talk about Deter, we must make sure the cost is there for the adversary — the cost in terms of time, space, assets and sustainment. You don't play around with Malaysia."

Malek said Deny involved preventing an adversary from achieving its objectives if it entered Malaysia's forward, extended or core areas, requiring the army, navy and air force to perform their roles across different operational domains.
He said Defeat would come into play if a threat reached the point where it had to be confronted, with the armed forces required to have the capability to defeat threats across all domains.
"If they enter, we must have the force to defeat them.
"This is not only about cyber, electromagnetic, media and information warfare, but also air, sea and land combat. We have to be ready across all domains."
The 5D approach was not merely an aspiration, but formed part of the Future Force strategy for dealing with current and future threats until 2055, he said.
"This is not just a hope. We have made it the Future Force strategy to face whatever threats and situations that exist now and in the future.
"We have to look at what is expected through 2055 and make sure the force we develop is credible and capable of facing it."
He said the Future Force programme began in 2021, with its first phase focused on designing the force, including its structure, organisation and strategy, while identifying gaps and weaknesses.
The second phase, from 2026 to 2030, focuses on force development, with the ultimate aim of creating a credible joint force that can respond to future threats.
BUILDING THE FORCE FOR FUTURE THREATS
Malek said capability development under the 2026-2030 phase of the Future Force would focus on ensuring readiness translated into credible deterrence.
"Readiness is deterrence. If you want to do something bad to Malaysia, you should think two or three times, maybe 10 times, before you come."
For the army, he said, priorities included mobility, protection and firepower, with new vehicles and systems to replace ageing platforms.
He added that the force also needed improved mortar and artillery firepower, short-range and very short-range air defence systems, communications, logistics and ammunition.
"The conflicts that we see, whether in the Middle East or Ukraine, show us that air defence is important, especially against missiles and drones.
"We have to make sure our air defence capability can counter the threats that we may face."
For the Royal Malaysian Navy, capability development includes the Littoral Combat Ship, Littoral Mission Ship Batch 2 and Fast Interceptor Craft programmes.
Malek said the Multi-Role Support Ship was particularly important for moving troops and assets between the peninsula, Sabah and Sarawak and was expected to be considered under the 13th Malaysia Plan.
"It gives us the strategic mobility to move the force where it is needed."
He highlighted plans for a new naval base in Bintulu to support operations in the country's fourth maritime region and strengthen the navy's presence in the South China Sea.
For the Royal Malaysian Air Force, the next five years will focus on a modernisation exercise to replace obsolete fighter aircraft, with the FA-50M forming part of the replacement programme.
Malek said the air force was also pursuing a Medium Range Air Defence System programme and additional radar capabilities to address surveillance gaps, particularly in Sabah and Sarawak.

He said three Anka unmanned aerial systems (drones) had already been activated in Labuan to strengthen forward surveillance in Sabah and Sarawak, while additional units could be considered under the next phases of the 13th Malaysia Plan, subject to government approval.
"We already have three Ankas in Labuan and they are being used for forward surveillance.
"For additional units, the requirement has been submitted and we are waiting for the government's approval."
He said the Bintulu Bare Base would serve as a forward operating base, allowing aircraft to operate closer to areas of interest without having to return to the main base in Kuching.
He said the facility was expected to be completed in 2028.
"We need a forward operating base so that our aircraft can move forward and operate closer to the area of operations.
"They do not have to return all the way to the main base every time, so this gives us greater operational flexibility."

On Station Lima on Pulau Layang-Layang, Malek said the armed forces would continue to improve facilities and infrastructure, including to the jetty, while maintaining the presence and readiness needed to safeguard Malaysia's extended maritime area.
He said the overall objective was to ensure the armed forces could translate its strategy into operational capability across the country's forward, extended and core areas.
"We have to make sure whatever strategy we adopt, we have the capability to execute it.
"That is what the Future Force is all about — making sure we are ready for the threats of today and tomorrow."

414a107a222d51b6: PETALING JAYA: Semangat Persekutuan perlu diterjemahkan secara lebih adil bagi memastikan pembangunan dan peluang ekonomi dinikmati secara seimbang antara negeri serta wilayah, kata Presiden Parti Wawasan Negara (Wawasan) Hamzah Zainudin.
Dalam perutusan sempena Hari Malaysia, Hamzah berkata kemajuan negara tidak seharusnya dinilai berdasarkan angka pertumbuhan semata-mata, sebaliknya mesti memberi kesan nyata kepada kehidupan rakyat.
“Kita mahu Malaysia yang lebih bersatu padu, Malaysia yang lebih makmur dan Malaysia yang lebih berjaya.
“Sebuah negara yang tidak hanya mengejar angka pertumbuhan, tetapi memastikan kemajuan itu benar-benar dirasai rakyat dengan memastikan semangat Persekutuan diterjemahkan dengan lebih adil,” katanya.

Beliau yang juga ketua pembangkang berkata pendekatan itu perlu disertai pembangunan lebih seimbang antara negeri dan wilayah, peluang ekonomi lebih luas serta sikap lebih prihatin terhadap keperluan rakyat.

Hamzah turut mengemukakan gagasan 'RESET Malaysia', yang menurutnya bukan bermaksud menolak segala yang telah dibina, tetapi memperbaiki perkara tidak lagi berkesan, menghentikan perkara merugikan dan membina semula perkara diperlukan untuk masa depan.
Menurutnya, meskipun rakyat berbeza kaum, agama, negeri dan pandangan politik, mereka perlu mempunyai titik temu mengenai bentuk Malaysia yang mahu dibina dan diwariskan kepada generasi akan datang.
Beliau menggariskan tiga perkara sebagai asas kepada usaha itu, iaitu matlamat bersama, kemakmuran bersama dan tadbir urus berperikemanusiaan.
Hamzah berkata matlamat bersama perlu memastikan keharmonian negara berkekalan, patriotisme dan kedaulatan terjamin, ekonomi kukuh serta Malaysia terus dihormati dunia.

Bagi kemakmuran bersama pula, beliau mahu manfaat ekonomi sampai ke seluruh negara menerusi lebih banyak peluang pekerjaan, peningkatan pendapatan isi rumah dan kehidupan lebih bermaruah untuk rakyat.
Beliau turut menegaskan kuasa kerajaan mesti digunakan untuk berkhidmat, bukan sekadar memerintah, manakala setiap dasar perlu mengambil kira realiti kehidupan rakyat.
“Rumah yang perlu sentiasa dipelihara, dibaiki dan diperkukuhkan. Masa depan rumah ini tanggungjawab kita bersama,” katanya merujuk Malaysia sebagai rumah bersama rakyat.
03de850dda2b70d2: KUALA LUMPUR: The armed forces have established a nucleus team to spearhead the formation of a Cyber Force, which is targeted to become operational by 2030.

Armed Forces chief General Tan Sri Malek Razak Sulaiman said the fourth service was necessary as cyberspace and electromagnetic warfare had become critical domains in modern security and military operations, with regional neighbours and other countries already developing similar capabilities.
"Last year, we established the nucleus team as part of our future force planning. The team will plan and assess the steps needed to turn the Cyber Force operational.

"The Defence Ministry has agreed to our guidelines. The aim is to have an operational Cyber Force by 2030 to carry out its duties in this domain," he said in an exclusive interview with the New Straits Times for the 93rd Armed Forces Day.
He said Defence Minister Datuk Seri Mohamed Khaled Nordin was expected to launch the nucleus team during the Armed Forces Day celebrations at the Lumut Naval Base on Saturday.
He said capability development in cyber and electromagnetic activities (CEMA) was underway, covering cyber operations, electronic warfare and spectrum management.
"These capabilities have been applied during Exercise Camar Kilat Series 2/26 to generate operational effects within the CEMA framework.
"The armed forces are also building a pool of CEMA specialists, with 60 air force officers and 17 from other ranks having attended related courses up to July."
In July, Khaled told the Dewan Negara that work was underway to establish the Cyber Force as the fourth service branch of the armed forces to counter threats from modern and cognitive warfare.
He said warfare had shifted from traditional physical combat to dominance in cyberspace and shaping public perception.
608fce6accef18ce: NEW YORK: Oil prices jumped, US bond yields rallied and equities retreated Tuesday as the Federal Reserve looked set to raise interest rates, with high inflation and AI concerns dominating market sentiment.

Brent crude futures again pushed towards US$110 a barrel, while average diesel prices in the US struck a record high of just under US$6.27 a gallon, heaping pressure on President Donald Trump ahead of midterm congressional elections.

"There's no let-up in the volatility rippling through financial markets, with energy prices staying painfully elevated and worries swirling about the knock-on effect for inflation and interest rates," said Susannah Streeter, chief investment strategist at Wealth Club.
The yield on the 10-year US Treasury note hit 5.03%, a level last seen in 2007 before the global financial crisis, as investors price in a likely hike in US interest rates.

The US Federal Reserve began a rate-setting meeting Tuesday with markets expecting policymakers to pull the trigger on a hike to tackle persistently high consumer prices in the world's biggest economy.
Market expectations for a 25-basis-point rate increase have risen sharply after official data published last week showed US annual inflation remaining far above the Fed's target.
With the crisis in the Middle East showing little sign of abating and Yemen's Houthi rebels taking control of a crucial outlet for shipping, crude has spiked this month to more than US$100 a barrel.
The surge in energy costs has ramped up pressure on central banks to raise borrowing costs.
The European Central Bank last week lifted interest rates in the eurozone.
The Bank of England is forecast to maintain its benchmark rate on Thursday as the UK economy struggles for growth.
Major Wall Street indices spent the session in the red following losses in Europe and Asia. The broad-based S&P 500 finished down 0.5%.

"The heavier cost of capital, rising fuel charges and worries about the potentially adverse societal impact of AI's rapid adoption have pushed stocks to their weakest prices in roughly six weeks ahead of tomorrow’s Fed decision," said a note from Jose Torres of Interactive Brokers.
If Fed policymakers vote to hike on Wednesday, it will be the first time the Fed has raised rates since 2023, when the central bank was still battling post-pandemic inflation.
Such a move will be sure to anger Trump, who has launched an unprecedented campaign to pressure the independent central bank to lower rates in order to spur economic activity.

f19d4a446a19c9d4: KUALA LUMPUR: A total of 100,904 armed forces personnel have declared their assets as the military tightens oversight of high-risk positions and strengthens safeguards against corruption and misconduct.

Armed Forces chief General Tan Sri Malek Razak Sulaiman told the New Straits Times that asset declarations had reached 97.53 per cent, while personnel in high-risk positions, including those involved in procurement, equipment specifications and financial management, would face closer monitoring.

The measures come amid heightened scrutiny of the armed forces following controversies earlier this year, including corruption cases involving senior military officers and allegations of immoral activities at military camps, which prompted internal investigations.

Earlier this year, former armed forces chief Tan Sri Mohd Nizam Jaffar was charged with abuse of power, criminal breach of trust and bribery, while former army chief Tan Sri Muhammad Hafiz-uddeain Jantan and his wife were charged with money laundering.

Also in the dock were former Malaysian Defence Intelligence Organisation chief Lieutenant-General Datuk Mohd Razali Alias and Joint Forces Headquarters chief of staff Major-General Datuk Mohamed Fauzi Kamis, who were charged with criminal breach of trust over an unauthorised welfare fund investment.
"Asset declaration in the armed forces is given serious attention. It's a true manifestation of honesty and trustworthiness.
"We have achieved 97.53 per cent, involving 100,904 officers and personnel," said Malek.
"I have also redeclared my assets after being appointed armed forces chief. All service personnel, senior officers and unit commanders were required to declare their assets.

"My KPI (key performance indicator) is that by Sept 16, all commanders, from the unit level up to the highest level, will have declared their assets," he said in an exclusive interview with the New Straits Times for the 93rd Armed Forces Day.
Malek said the 2026-2030 Anti-Corruption Action Plan had been implemented, while the Integrity and Anti-Corruption Plan was being developed to strengthen governance and corruption prevention.
He said officers holding high-risk positions would be reviewed within 18 months, with commanders and senior officers assessing their suitability and effectiveness in the posts.
"If they are no longer suitable, they will be transferred.

"But if they are effective and still required based on their subject matter expertise, commanders can recommend that they remain in the position, subject to the highest level of integrity monitoring."
He said the approach was to ensure officers in sensitive positions remained under continuous scrutiny, rather than relying solely on fixed-term rotations.
He said governance compliance would be continuously monitored by the Defence Ministry's Integrity Unit and governance monitoring units at the respective service headquarters.
These include the inspector-general departments at the Armed Forces Headquarters and the army, navy and air force, alongside auditors and audit officers at field formations.
Malek added that checks and balances were further strengthened through the Malaysian Armed Forces Standard Management Audit, including unannounced audits.

"Governance involving assets, finances, security and human resources must remain transparent and comply with regulations, with every audit finding requiring immediate corrective action and improvements.

"A total of 105,536 officers and personnel, or 98.7 per cent of the total active workforce, have also completed the Anti-Corruption Pledge, while integrity modules have been conducted for 4,240 personnel at 26 training centres."
He said moral and spiritual development of personnel was also being strengthened, with character-building part of the effort.

He said this included the 3T module — Takhalli, Tahalli and Tajalli — which focuses on removing negative traits and practices, instilling good values and character and translating values into actions and exemplary conduct.

He said the armed forces also strengthened the Islamic Spiritual Division, formerly known as the Armed Forces Religious Corps (Kagat), by placing it under his purview to give it greater organisational weight.
"A dedicated cell has also been established to address the spiritual welfare of non-Muslim personnel according to their faiths.

"Kagat officers were exposed to strategic thinking and defence studies, including through greater participation in staff colleges, so that they can contribute beyond religious duties and bring a spiritual and ethical perspective to wider organisational and strategic matters.
"We do not want our religious officers to become only tok siak, tok bilal or imam.
"I want them to develop strategic thinking so they can contribute to building the armed forces, together with strong human capital grounded in spirituality."
