1ee03530ff58d9f3: KOTA KINABALU/KUALA LUMPUR, Sept 16 — Julia Chan and Arif Zikri spoke to Sabahans and Sarawakians on what Malaysia means to them and what it means to be Malaysian.
The Sabah perspective

Ask Sabahans about being Malaysian and they can begin with something as uncomplicated and universal as good food and world class sunsets and end with something much more complicated: how to belong to a diverse federation without losing the unique identity that comes with being Sabahan.

Ahead of Malaysia Day, Malay Mail asked several Sabahans what comes to mind when they hear “Malaysia”, what being Malaysian means to them, how that identity differs in Sabah, and what they wish people in Peninsular Malaysia understood about being Sabahan.
What comes to mind when you hear “Malaysia”?
For many, including marine biologist Malinda Auluck, 40, the answer was first and foremost food — and the strong opinions that come with it.
“We are snobbish about our food. Want to cause an uproar? Ask for crispy skin rendang,” she said.
Comedian and trivia host Matt Brian, 29, had a more unexpected first thought.
“To be honest, as a comedian, the first thing I thought of was the missing plane,” he said.
Most waxed lyrical about Malaysia’s delectable food and cultural diversity although corruption was another answer, albeit one given in jest.
But jokes aside, Malaysia meant home and Sabahans loved the country’s diversity and the ability of people from different races and cultures to live alongside one another, mostly in peace.
“It’s far from perfect, but I can say it’s got the best food in the world, it’s got the best sunsets in the world, and the best people. That works for me,” Matt said.
For digital marketer Leon Kuan, 33, Malaysia brought to mind food, cultural diversity, multiple languages and the Malaysia Agreement 1963, which paved the way for the formation of the federation.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Leon, 33, feels Sabah is still misunderstood by West Malaysians and needs to be given the same respect within the Federation. — Picture by Julia Chan
What does being Malaysian mean to you?

For the Sabahans interviewed, being Malaysian was closely tied to the experience of growing up surrounded by different cultures, languages and traditions so deeply integrated into daily life that navigating them requires little conscious thought.
“The ability to move comfortably between different cultures, languages and traditions is not something I consciously practise because it has become second nature,” said Malinda.
For psychiatrist Liang Yoong, 33, being Malaysian meant being born and raised in the country while identifying with its many cultures, cuisines and languages through shared experiences.
For entrepreneur Dinoza Mahruf, 51, diversity was what made Malaysia distinctive.
“For me, being Malaysian means being proud to call home a country where diversity is our identity and unity is our strength,” he said.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Sandra, 50, says being Sabahan was part of her identity and is proud of her Sabahan roots. — Picture courtesy of Sandra Sokial
Civil servant Sandra Sokial, 50, described it as being part of “a bigger family” while remaining proud of where she came from.
“I believe that being Malaysian should not mean having to set aside my Sabahan identity,” she said.
Other answers included Malaysia’s strong passport, its affordability relative to the standard of living, government subsidies and assistance, and the warm hospitality associated with Malaysians.
Does being Malaysian mean something different in Sabah?
For the Sabahans interviewed, the answer was broadly yes — but not because they felt less Malaysian.
Rather, they described a Malaysian identity in Sabah shaped by its particularly diverse population and a culture of accommodation between communities.
Liang said Sabah had “a special kind of understanding and acceptance” that she felt was not always found in Peninsular Malaysia.
“We accept the differences and the similarities, we readily accommodate instead of insisting on basing everything on our own race or religion,” she said.
Brian described Sabah as a more “idealistic” and relaxed society.
“We’re very, very united. We’re very chill, Sabahan amalgamation. We’re tight, and we don’t take things too seriously down here in Sabah,” he said.
He said people of different religions and backgrounds could share the same spaces without necessarily making an issue of what others ate or drank.
“We’re just living our own lives. We’re very, very chill,” he said.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

Matt Brian, 29, a comedian cum trivia host, believes Sabahans are 'chill" about race relations, and don't want interference from their Peninsula Malaysian counterparts. — Picture courtesy of Matt Brian
That cultural fluidity is also evident in the way Sabahans communicate, said Rozzy Rajab, 39.

She recalled travelling to Kuala Lumpur for a company event with another native Sabahan, where the two naturally switched between Sabah Malay and Mandarin while chatting with a West Malaysian make-up artist.
The make-up artist was surprised by how naturally they moved between the two languages, which Rozzy said was common and unremarkable in Sabah.
She added that Sabah’s ethnic identities could also be difficult for outsiders to neatly categorise.
“Some Kadazans look very much like Chinese and some Chinese look very Bumiputera,” she said, pointing out that people in West Malaysia were often viewed through racial lenses.

Leon, who lived in Kuala Lumpur for several years, said the level of “halal pettiness/toleration” was very different between East and West Malaysia, although Sabah also had its own sensitivities and points of contention.
For Malinda, the Sabahan experience also meant being more conscious of inequalities within Malaysia.

“For me, the biggest difference is the sense of privilege. Growing up in Sabah, the development gap is much more visible, so you're constantly aware that access to infrastructure, education, healthcare and opportunities isn't equal for everyone.

“I don't know if someone who has only lived in big cities like Kuala Lumpur and Selangor would notice this in the same way, because many of those conveniences are simply part of everyday life there,” she said.
What is one thing you wish West Malaysians understood about being Sabahan?

The answers varied, but a common thread emerged: Sabahans do not want their identity reduced to race, religion or politics — and being proud to be Sabahan should never be interpreted as being less Malaysian.
For auditor Peter Wong, 35, it came down to “tolerance and understanding”.
“Not everything revolves around race, religion and politics,” he said.
Brian was even more direct.
“Don’t come here with your identity politics,” he said.
“Don’t try to split us up according to race, according to religion, according to political party. We don’t need that. We’re doing just fine.”
For Rozzy, one thing she wished Peninsular Malaysians understood was Sabah’s relatively easy-going relationship between different faiths and communities.
She said people in Sabah were generally accustomed to celebrating together and respecting each other’s practices without making every interaction a religious issue.

“Definitely don’t come here and cause trouble. Muslims and non Muslims in Sabah are very tolerant towards each other and non judgemental. We celebrate the festivities without issue and genuine celebrated our differences,” she said.
Malinda pointed to another big misconception — that Sabah’s lower level of development meant the cost of living was cheaper.
“In reality, many things are just as expensive, if not more expensive, than in the Peninsula. That’s something many Sabahans live with every day,” she said.
She also pointed to the high cost of travelling between Sabah and the Peninsula, particularly airfares.

Leon, meanwhile, pointed to Sabah’s constitutional position and the Malaysia Agreement 1963. He said many Sabahans struggled to be viewed as equal to their West Malaysian counterparts, whether at a personal or political level.
“When you mention Malaysia, Peninsular people will mention August 31 as National Day. But September 16, the day Malaysia was formed, is not given the same prominence,” he said.

He argued that Sabah and Sarawak should not simply be viewed in the same way as the other states in the federation, reflecting the long-running Sabah and Sarawak position on their status and rights under MA63.
Sandra similarly said Sabahans had their own history and perspective on the formation of Malaysia.
“We see ourselves not simply as another state, but as one of the partners that formed Malaysia, and that shapes how we understand our place in the federation,” she said.
“For many Sabahans, this is not about being less Malaysian. It is about being recognised as an equal partner and having our position respected.”
Dinoza’s message to Peninsular Malaysians was simpler.
“We are Malaysians too,” he said.
There was plenty of pride in Malaysia — its food, diversity, hospitality, shared languages and the ability of people from different backgrounds to live alongside one another.

But there was also a clear desire for that Malaysian identity to accommodate the particular experience of being Sabahan — one shaped by geography, development gaps, cultural fluidity and a different understanding of Malaysia’s formation.
For those interviewed, being Sabahan and being Malaysian were not competing identities.
As Sandra put it: “Being proud to be Sabahan does not make us less Malaysian.”
A strong sense of belonging
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Multi-award-winning songstress Dayang Nurfaizah, born and raised in Kuching, said that Malaysia is home above all else. — Picture via Instagram
Merdeka Day honours the legacy of 1957, but Malaysia Day marks the union that completed the country.
Malay Mail sat down with several Sarawakian celebrities to explore heritage, identity, and the Bornean pride shaping modern Malaysia.
Multi-award-winning songstress Dayang Nurfaizah, born and raised in Kuching, said that Malaysia is home above all else.
“The food, the people, everything is so warm and colourful.
“Even with all our differences, somehow it all just..works,” Dayang said.
She added that for her, being a Malaysian means celebrating unity in diversity and growing up with different races, languages and cultures is something that she takes pride in.
70666dfdfb95d577: COLOMBO, Sept 16 — Sri Lanka’s famed seafood shack Beach Wadiya has hosted royalty including Britain’s Princess Anne and sporting legends such as cricketer Sachin Tendulkar, but now faces demolition under a government-ordered coastal clean-up.

The simple Colombo beach restaurant has welcomed a string of celebrities, featured in Madhur Jaffrey’s culinary travels and received rave reviews in international publications, including London’s Financial Times.
“Beach Wadiya comes with a lot of history,” said Suhara Chandrasekera, the founder’s granddaughter, now a director of the restaurant.
But more than half a century after it opened, the glamour is giving way to grief at Wadiya — which means “shack” in the island’s Sinhala language.
The government’s Coast Conservation and Coastal Resource Management Department gave Wadiya 10 days to pack up and leave — or face demolition.
That deadline expired on September 10, but the restaurant is resisting the order to leave.
Seven other beach properties were given extensions of about four days to salvage furniture and fittings.
A few shops near Wadiya were demolished last month as part of a broader government plan to remove businesses within 10 metres (33 feet) of the shoreline.
“There shouldn’t be any buildings within the 10-metre coastal reservation from the shoreline,” Environment Minister Dammika Patabendi told AFP.
“We have identified 82 such premises and we are taking steps to remove them.”
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Co‑owner Suhara Chandrasekera shows a celebrity photo album at Colombo’s Beach Wadiya shack. — AFP pic
‘Sea erosion’
Beach Wadiya is the only establishment resisting the order and has taken the matter to court.
The family of its late founder, Olwyn Weerasekera, argues that the restaurant existed before the 1981 Coast Conservation Act being used to evict them.
“We built in 1974, which predates the law that they were talking about... We have permits dating all the way back to 1974,” 26-year-old Chandrasekera said.
“In addition to the appeal to the Coast Conservation Department, we also took the decision to file a writ,” she told AFP, referring to a case filed in the Court of Appeal.
The family has won a temporary reprieve, with the court ordering the department not to demolish the restaurant for two weeks pending a hearing.
When Wadiya was established, the beach was wider and cleaner, with rows of coconut trees, most of which have since been lost to sea erosion.
“Right now we have lost two of our huts... We’ve lost parts of our bathroom due to sea erosion,” Chandrasekera said.
She said Wadiya was the only restaurant on the beach before Sri Lanka’s tourism boom in the late 1970s.
Princess Anne had dinner at Wadiya in 1995. Nepali royals have also dined there.

British tycoon Richard Branson visited the restaurant during a family holiday in Sri Lanka in 1992, although the guestbook he signed was washed away in the December 2004 tsunami, according to the family.
Indian singing sensation Asha Bhosle, and cricket stars including India’s Rahul Dravid and former Pakistan skipper Wasim Akram, have also dined there.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Seafood shack Beach Wadiya. — AFP pic
Singing lobster
One of the restaurant’s walls has a reproduction of a Financial Times cartoon of a guitar-playing lobster that accompanied a March 1994 food review headlined: “Cook me tender.”
The restaurant is best known for offering diners a platter of fresh seafood from which they can choose how it should be cooked.
There is no air conditioning and small tables are set up on the beach. An upper floor was added as the beachfront shrank over the years.
Experts blame worsening erosion on large-scale land reclamation farther north near Colombo port.
If the courts allow the restaurant to survive the government’s coastal clean-up, Chandrasekera says Wadiya will return to its roots.
“The only restaurant on the strip,” she said. — AFP
0227530c035b6459: BERLIN, Sept 16 — Politicians campaigning for Sunday’s Berlin state election have painted an unflattering picture of the German capital, vowing to clear garbage-strewn streets and promising “syringe-free playgrounds”.

Town hall-hopefuls have also pledged to clean up graffiti-covered train stations, end “forever-building sites”, fix buckled cycling lanes and take steps to ease a desperate shortage of affordable housing.
Taken together, the list of woes hardens the image of a chronically broke city whose administration often struggles to reliably provide services for its almost four million people.
Certainly, many who live in Berlin love its rich artistic and cultural life, green spaces, lakes and children’s playgrounds, vibrant start-up scene and hedonistic, anything-goes nightlife.
The long-divided city boasts countless museums, galleries and sites reflecting its troubled history, as well as two zoos, three opera houses and multiple techno clubs known around the world.

But all of that has gone hand-in-hand with persistent complaints about a slow bureaucracy and a dysfunctional city administration which famously took almost 15 years to build an international airport with next-door Brandenburg state.
Cross-financed by Germany’s wealthier states, Berlin is deep in the red, with 2.2 billion euros in debt calculated in late 2024, which forced painful spending cuts in multiple areas.
Berlin’s former mayor Klaus Wowereit once famously labelled Berlin “poor but sexy” — but since then many of its residents have at times struggled to stay in love with the city.
‘Garbage mountains’

Local newspapers often write about Berlin’s “crime hotspots” and rising homelessness, and make great sport of documenting ever-new Berlin disasters — from rat-infested police stations to the closure of the Technical University’s main campus due to structural defects and fire safety issues.
With renovations now set to cost around 2.4 billion euros, university president Fatma Deniz blamed “decades of delayed investment and budget cuts in public infrastructure”.

The small party Volt has been running campaign posters with the promise to “unf*** berlin” that list a litany of complaints from potholes to “garbage mountains” and, more generally, “Berlin frustration”.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
A homeless person in a sleeping bag lies on the stairs of the Anhalter Bahnhof S-Bahn public transport commuter train station in Berlin on February 23, 2026. — AFP pic
One Berlin resident fed up with filthy streets has taken matters into her own hands.

Valeriia Tantcyreva, 31, started the volunteer group Sauberberlin (Clean Berlin), which on a recent outing in the working-class district of Wedding filled a secure disposal box with syringes discarded by drug users.
“No one cares about the city,” she charged, calling the waste management service “useless”. She said she decided to take action after her dog was repeatedly injured by broken glass and other refuse.
City hall told AFP, when asked about the garbage problem, that there were “no operational failures”, pointing instead to many residents’ lack of civic responsibility.
Another pet peeve for many are sketchy cycling lanes in a city where 18 per cent of all trips are made by bike.
They are often “outdated, too narrow, overgrown with vegetation and buckled by tree roots”, complained Lisa Feitsch of the cycling association ADFC.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
A commuter walks along a passage at the Wannsee S-Bahn train station which is out of service on January 4, 2026. — AFP pic
‘Chaos city’
The city’s politics may be even messier than its streets, and the next government is certain to again be run by a multi-party coalition.
Four parties are leading the race for the Rotes Rathaus (Red Town Hall), all polling in the range of 16 to 21 per cent, with the centre-left SPD trailing behind them.
Frontrunners for the top spot are the centre-right CDU — which is strongest in Berlin’s leafy western suburbs — and the far-left Die Linke, whose heartland lies in parts of the former east.
The far-right AfD, whose bastion is among the communist-era residential tower blocks of the former East Berlin, expects new record results — but also to remain shut out of power by all other parties.
Also among the top four are the Greens, who dominate in hip inner-city areas known for trendy cafes, organic supermarkets and cargo bicycles.
When Berlin voters head to the polls on Sunday, they will hope to elect a capable new government — but also simply that the city-state doesn’t mess up the vote itself, like it did in 2021.
Citizens back then waited in hours-long queues while some polling booths ran out of ballot papers and resupplies were obstructed by a marathon the city had decided to stage on the same day.
The 2021 election fiasco, as well as subsequent street unrest on New Year’s Eve, led the Bavarian state premier Markus Soeder, based in far tidier Munich, to thunder that Berlin was a “chaos city”.
Berlin eventually held a successful re-run of the vote in 2023. — AFP
2280f2985e89348e: BEIJING, Sept 16 — From a distance, it looks as though a giant spaceship has just landed in the palm tree-dotted streets near downtown Los Angeles.
It could also be a wide-canopied tree or a low passing cloud — but for its Chinese architect Ma Yansong, as long as the building “sparks curiosity”, he’s achieved his purpose.
Over the past two decades, Ma has created dozens of visually striking projects in his home country and abroad, integrating nature with sleek, modern designs.

In some ways, his seemingly sci-fi-inspired style is a perfect match for his newest project opening on September 22, the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art in Los Angeles, founded by Star Wars creator George Lucas and his wife, Mellody Hobson.
“The building takes on a futuristic feel that generates excitement,” Ma told AFP at the Beijing office of MAD Architects, the firm he established in 2004.
“When people visit the Lucas Museum, they will each bring their own unique perspectives,” said the 50-year-old, who last year was included on Time magazine’s list of the 100 most influential people.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Chinese architect and founder of MAD Architects Ma Yansong. — AFP pic
“They might catch a beam of light, see it cutting through the building, glimpse the clouds, the sky, or even the cosmos.
“This sparks curiosity and new ideas — and those diverse thoughts are incredibly valuable.”
Mountains and water
A Beijing native, he grew up in a courtyard house typical of the “hutong” alleyways that crisscross the historic centre of China’s capital city.
“There was a very close connection to nature,” he said, recalling the trees and small pockets of open space interspersed in hutong neighbourhoods.
Later, he went overseas to train as an architect, graduating from the Yale School of Architecture and working briefly at the studio of acclaimed Iraqi-British designer Zaha Hadid.
Ma and his firm have conceptualised landmark works all over China, including the Harbin Opera House, a vast, swooping structure perched dramatically on the banks of the frigid Songhua River.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
A view of Chaoyang Park Plaza, designed by MAD Architects and inspired by traditional ‘shanshui’ Chinese landscape paintings. — AFP pic

Abroad, his notable projects include a pair of twisting residential buildings called the “Absolute Towers” near Toronto, Canada, and a migration-themed museum that opened last year in Rotterdam, the Netherlands.
Ma’s architectural vision draws inspiration from traditional Chinese paintings known as shanshui, or mountains and water, usually depicting natural scenery.
The Lucas Museum is closely interwoven with its external environment by lawns, trees, running water and a roof covered in vegetation and solar panels.
“If you look at a Chinese garden, it is a completely natural environment, even though it is artificially designed,” Ma told AFP.
“There is a global conversation (now) about ecology and how to bring people closer to nature, yet I find that traditional Eastern architecture mastered this long ago,” he said.
People-centred architecture
Ma told AFP that he embraces what he calls a “major shift” in architecture towards placing people, rather than the buildings themselves, at the centre of the design concept.
“We aren’t using architecture to flaunt wealth or power,” he said.
Although many of MAD’s clients wield significant financial resources, Ma said his focus is not merely to impress, but also to create “uniquely valuable space for people to enjoy”.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
A view of the Baiziwan Social Housing project. — AFP pic
MAD’s Beijing office is located in the heart of a hutong neighbourhood near where Ma attended school in his youth.
“I like these small streets, with their trees, the people walking by and that certain atmosphere of everyday urban life,” he said.

Ma said when he designs a building he wants to make sure it gives “freedom of movement” to residents — a concept which drove his design of the Baiziwan Social Housing project in Beijing, a subsidised residential compound for low-income communities.
“Many low-income individuals feel they cannot integrate into the city,” said Ma.
“Often, such housing is walled off, isolating residents,” he said, adding: “It’s a psychological barrier — they feel the city doesn’t accept them.”

Unlike the closed, block-like apartments that have sprung up in Chinese cities during decades of rapid urbanisation, Baiziwan features an open layout with an elevated garden level and a design that optimises sunlight.
Ma said he doesn’t want his buildings “to be a palace or a temple-like structure that demands reverence”.
“I want it to be open, a place where everyone feels they are the masters of the city.” — AFP
05c5765070a77df5: PETALING JAYA: One of Malaysia’s founding fathers, Tan Cheng Lock, was among the first leaders to articulate the need to instil a Malayan-centred political consciousness among the Malayan Chinese, says academic Toh Chen Chun.

In “One Country, One People: The Life and Legacy of Tun Tan Cheng Lock”, a biography of the MCA founder, Toh noted that Tan used his growing standing among the British to highlight the need for them to change their policies towards their Malayan subjects.

Toh, a co-author of the biography, said Tan spoke at length during a 1920 lunch with Straits Settlements governor Laurence Guillemard about the need to encourage Malaya’s “sons of the soil” to take a “livelier and more active interest in the welfare of the country of their birth”.
“Whether they are Malays, Eurasians, Indians or Chinese, they have made this country their permanent home.

“They are the sons of the soil, they are part and parcel of the empire whose governments and institutions are so firmly founded in the great and grand principles of liberty,” said Tan, who believed at the time that Malaya’s future was to be an autonomous part of the British empire.

Toh said it was thanks to this speech, during which Tan also strongly advocated the admission of Malayans into the civil service, that Guillemard later appointed him as an unofficial member of the Straits Settlements legislative council in 1923.
Tan used the opportunity to promote his political ideas at the council, and three years later unveiled his vision of a “self-governing British Malaya with a federal government and Parliament”.

In a speech in 1926, he called for Malaya’s leaders to “foster and create a true Malayan spirit and consciousness amongst its people” and to “build up a Malayan community with a Malayan consciousness”.
“Cheng Lock was one of the first leaders to articulate the need for all Malayans to think of themselves as Malayans first instead of prioritising their ethnic groups.

“In contrast to the rise of Malay nationalism among the Malays and China-centred nationalism among the Chinese, Cheng Lock strongly advocated a Malayan-centred self-governing political entity,” Toh said.

Toh noted, however, that inculcating this vision in the Malayan Chinese community was an uphill battle for Tan, who found it easier to convince the English-educated elite of his concept of a “Malayan consciousness”.

He said the “Laukehs” and “Sinkehs” – terms referring respectively to the first wave of mass Chinese immigrants who came to Malaya before the mid-19th century and the more recent arrivals after World War I – regarded Malaya as a temporary place to earn money before retiring to their ancestral villages in China.
“As a Peranakan, Cheng Lock could not speak Mandarin or any Chinese dialect. This made it hard for him to convince both Laukehs and Sinkehs to accept his concept of a Malayan consciousness.
“Given their China-centric orientation, Cheng Lock found it difficult to appeal to them to participate in local politics and regard Malaya as their home,” he said.

It was later in 1951, when Malayan politicians, including Umno founder Onn Jaafar, agreed to grant citizenship to all non-Malays born in Malaya, that Tan argued that the “only effective way of weaning the China-born Chinese from being obsessed with Chinese national politics is to make a generous offer of Malayan citizenship”.
“One Country, One People: The Life and Legacy of Tun Tan Cheng Lock” is published by UTAR Press and can be purchased for RM130 by emailing alumni@tarc.edu.my.
All proceeds from the sales will be donated to the Tun Tan Siew Sin Student Loan Fund at TARUMT.
c4765f442220c28d: PETALING JAYA: Tan Cheng Lock, antara tokoh pengasas Malaysia menjadi sebahagian pemimpin terawal yang memperjuangkan kesedaran politik berteraskan identiti Malaya dalam kalangan masyarakat Cina di Tanah Melayu, kata ahli akademik Toh Chen Chun.

Dalam One Country, One People: The Life and Legacy of Tun Tan Cheng Lock, sebuah biografi mengenai pengasas MCA itu, Toh berkata Tan menggunakan pengaruhnya yang semakin meningkat dalam kalangan British untuk menekankan perlunya dasar terhadap penduduk Malaya diubah.

Toh, yang juga penulis bersama buku itu berkata, ketika menghadiri satu jamuan tengah hari bersama Gabenor Negeri-negeri Selat, Laurence Guillemard pada 1920, Tan bercakap panjang mengenai perlunya ‘anak watan’ Malaya digalakkan supaya lebih aktif mengambil berat tentang kebajikan negara tempat mereka dilahirkan.
“Tidak kira sama ada mereka Melayu, Eurasia, India atau Cina, mereka telah menjadikan negara ini sebagai kediaman tetap mereka.

“Mereka adalah anak watan, mereka sebahagian daripada empayar yang kerajaan dan institusinya dibina kukuh berasaskan prinsip kebebasan yang luhur,” kata Tan, yang ketika itu berpandangan masa depan Malaya adalah sebagai wilayah autonomi dalam Empayar British.

Toh berkata, ucapan itu yang turut menyaksikan Tan bersungguh-sungguh memperjuangkan kemasukan rakyat Malaya ke dalam perkhidmatan awam, mendorong Guillemard melantiknya sebagai ahli tidak rasmi Majlis Perundangan Negeri-negeri Selat pada 1923.

Tan kemudian menggunakan kedudukannya dalam majlis itu untuk mengetengahkan gagasan politiknya. Tiga tahun kemudian, beliau mengemukakan visinya bagi sebuah ‘Malaya British yang berkerajaan sendiri dengan kerajaan persekutuan dan Parlimen’.
Dalam ucapannya pada 1926, Tan menggesa pemimpin Malaya memupuk ‘semangat dan kesedaran Malaya yang sebenar’ dalam kalangan rakyat serta membina sebuah masyarakat yang mempunyai ‘kesedaran Malaya’.
“Cheng Lock antara pemimpin terawal yang menyuarakan keperluan supaya semua penduduk Malaya melihat diri mereka sebagai orang Malaya terlebih dahulu, bukannya mengutamakan kaum masing-masing.

“Ketika nasionalisme Melayu berkembang dalam kalangan orang Melayu dan nasionalisme berorientasikan China dalam kalangan masyarakat Cina, Cheng Lock pula kuat memperjuangkan sebuah entiti politik berkerajaan sendiri yang berteraskan Malaya,” kata Toh.

Namun, Toh berkata usaha Tan untuk menerapkan gagasan itu dalam kalangan masyarakat Cina di Malaya bukan mudah. Beliau mendapati golongan elit berpendidikan Inggeris lebih mudah menerima konsep ‘kesedaran Malaya’ yang dibawanya.

Katanya, golongan ‘Laukeh’ dan ‘Sinkeh’ masing-masing merujuk kepada gelombang awal pendatang Cina yang datang secara besar-besaran ke Malaya sebelum pertengahan abad ke-19 dan mereka yang tiba kemudian selepas Perang Dunia Pertama.
Kedua-dua kelompok itu melihat Malaya sebagai tempat sementara untuk mencari rezeki sebelum kembali menghabiskan usia di kampung halaman nenek moyang mereka di China.

“Sebagai seorang Peranakan, Cheng Lock tidak boleh bertutur dalam bahasa Mandarin atau mana-mana dialek Cina. Keadaan itu menyukarkannya untuk meyakinkan golongan Laukeh dan Sinkeh supaya menerima konsep ‘kesedaran Malaya’.
“Disebabkan orientasi mereka yang lebih tertumpu kepada China, Cheng Lock sukar meyakinkan mereka untuk terbabit dalam politik tempatan dan menganggap Malaya sebagai tanah air mereka,” katanya.

Pada 1951, apabila ahli politik Malaya termasuk pengasas Umno Onn Jaafar bersetuju memberikan kewarganegaraan kepada semua bukan Melayu yang dilahirkan di Malaya, Tan berhujah bahawa satu-satunya cara berkesan untuk mengalihkan perhatian masyarakat Cina kelahiran China daripada terlalu tertumpu kepada politik kebangsaan China adalah dengan menawarkan kewarganegaraan Malaya secara lebih terbuka.
One Country, One People: The Life and Legacy of Tun Tan Cheng Lock diterbitkan UTAR Press dan boleh dibeli pada harga RM130 dengan menghubungi alumni@tarc.edu.my menerusi e-mel.
Semua hasil jualan akan disumbangkan kepada Tabung Pinjaman Pelajar Tun Tan Siew Sin di TARUMT.

7ce89004f7643041: WASHINGTON: The United States on Tuesday announced new restrictions on visas for South Africans, after President Donald Trump repeatedly criticised the country's leaders over its post-apartheid racial justice policies.
Trump has lambasted South Africa's land and employment laws that are meant to redress stark inequalities that remain 30 years after the end of white-minority rule.

In 2025, he berated President Cyril Ramaphosa in the Oval Office over discredited claims of a "white genocide" in South Africa. He has also hit the country with high tariffs and boycotted a G20 summit in Johannesburg.

The new visa restrictions target South Africans who "enable uncompensated land seizures, race-based discrimination, and/or the incitement of imminent violence against members of minority ethnic or racial groups," the US State Department said.

Ties between the two nations have nosedived since Trump took office last year, with the US leader cutting aid, expelling the South African ambassador and offering "refuge" to South African whites fleeing "persecution."
While the US president has cracked down on immigration, he launched a scheme under which thousands of white Afrikaners have been allowed to settle in the United States.

South Africa said last month it would offer a "generous" new trade deal to the United States as it seeks to avoid hefty tariffs that threaten massive job losses on top of its dire unemployment crisis.
82c9f6f1d7986e16: WASHINGTON: Senate Democrats accused FBI Director Kash Patel at a fiery congressional hearing on Tuesday of abusing his position as head of the law enforcement agency to intimidate journalists.
Patel angrily rejected the allegations during the Senate Judiciary Committee hearing and lauded the FBI's record in reducing violent crime, fighting drug trafficking and prosecuting fraud.
Patel and several Democratic senators traded sharply personal attacks during the combative four-and-a-half-hour hearing.

"Like a thug, you're using your agency to go after reporters," said Senator Cory Booker, a Democrat from New Jersey. "Reporters wrote about the president and your bureau went to their homes and subpoenaed their mothers.
"A reporter wrote about you and your bureau ran her name through records and began an investigation," Booker added.
The FBI director said it was a "total lie" that he had used FBI resources to target reporters.
Patel filed a US$250 million suit in April against The Atlantic magazine and the author of an article he called a "defamatory hit piece."
The Atlantic story accused Patel of frequently drinking to excess and said he was in danger of losing his job as FBI director.
According to the cable news channel MS Now, the FBI launched a so-called "insider threat investigation" into the Atlantic story.
Since taking over as the head of the Federal Bureau of Investigation, Patel has been accused of carrying out a purge of agents perceived as being disloyal to President Donald Trump.
Among those dismissed have been scores of agents who worked on criminal cases brought against Trump after he left the White House in 2021.
Asked by senators about the wave of departures on Tuesday, Patel said "there was no purging" and the vast majority of the agents who left retired voluntarily.
The hearing also featured a series of bizarre exchanges over the FBI's decision to lift restrictions on hiring of applicants who have engaged in prostitution or bestiality.

"The FBI has lowered its hiring standards by dropping automatic disqualification for applicants who have stolen from prior employers, paid for sex, or engaged in bestiality," said Senator Dick Durbin, a Democrat from Illinois.
Patel said this refers to applicants who were victims not perpetrators.

"Applicants who have engaged in bestiality means they were victims of bestiality because they were forced to do so," he said. "We did not want to punish victims of bestiality, victims who were trafficked."
The FBI director also raised concerns among Democrats by declining to rule out sending agents to polling places during the November midterm elections.
"Election integrity is of paramount importance," he said. "This FBI is not going to shy away from that effort."

AFTER more than a year of training for one of the world's toughest ultra-trails, Gunung Kinabalu porter Daved Simpat crossed the finish line in Chamonix, France — carrying far more than just a personal achievement.
The 44-year-old completed the gruelling 174km Ultra-Trail du Mont-Blanc in 28 hours, 53 minutes and four seconds last month.
The feat reflects the strength, discipline and perseverance Daved developed while carrying climbers' loads up and down the mountain.
"Gunung Kinabalu has shaped me and is part of my life," he told the 'New Straits Times'.
At 4,095m above sea level, Gunung Kinabalu has served as Daved's workplace and training ground for most of his adult life.
The same principles he adopted for Gunung Kinabalu apply to ultra-trail — knowing when to run and when to walk, conserving energy and, most importantly, refusing to give up when the going gets tough.
As the first of seven Malaysians to cross the finish line after almost 29 hours, his thoughts turned to family, friends and those who had supported him.
The father of two from Kampung Himbaan in Ranau hopes his achievement inspires fellow porters and Sabah's youngsters.
Daved takes pride in his roots as a porter and does not view it merely as a stepping stone to becoming an international athlete.
"I want to show that our background is not a barrier. From a mountain in Sabah, a porter can also stand on one of the biggest ultra-trail stages in the world."
Daved said he was proud to bring the names of Sabah and Malaysia to the international stage.
He believes Sabah has much to offer — from its mountains and forests to its talented people and untapped potential.
His message to the young people in Sabah is simple: dream big, regardless of where you come from or what you do for a living.

For Daved, going from carrying heavy loads on Gunung Kinabalu to completing one of the world's toughest races proves that hard work, confidence and perseverance can take you further than you ever imagined.

74fb4ce557137c45: BOGOTA: Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella fired his statistics chief after the official ruled out inconsistencies in unemployment figures under the previous government, the former director said Tuesday.
De la Espriella took office in August and has accused his predecessor Gustavo Petro, Colombia's first-ever leftist leader, of corruption.
The president announced the dismissal of Ricardo Valencia as head of the national statistics agency (DANE) in a statement on Monday, barely three weeks after appointing him.
"I didn't have any communication from the presidency or from the president expressing any dissatisfaction," Valencia told Bogota-based Blu Radio on Tuesday.
A remark at a press conference cost him his job, it turned out.
Valencia responded to a journalist's question saying that he had not found any inconsistencies in labour market indicators during July, when Petro was still president.
"Up until the date when they asked me that question, I had not found any irregularities," the economist said.
De la Espriella has made it compulsory for all ministries and government agencies to seek permission from the presidency before providing any information to the press.
The presidency criticised Valencia for claiming not to have found "any irregularities" in the data "without having first carried out thorough audits."
Following the dismissal of their director, the DANE workers' union on Tuesday voiced concern about the agency's independence.

THE number of hotspots detected in Kalimantan has surged to 808, which may cause transboundary haze to spread in the region.
Malaysian Meteorological Department (MetMalaysia) director-general Dr Mohd Hisham Mohd Anip said this depended on the extent of open burning in Indonesia and wind conditions.
"As long as the fires are not extinguished, the haze situation will continue to affect neighbouring countries.
"We are in the southwest monsoon period, during which winds blow from Indonesia towards our country. It is expected to end only in October."
Data from the Asean Specialised Meteorological Centre (ASMC) showed that the number of hotspots in Kalimantan rose from 301 on Saturday to 461 the next day before surging to 808 on Monday.
During the same period, ASMC also recorded 87 hotspots in Sumatra, 15 in Sabah and Sarawak, and one in Peninsular Malaysia.
However, it said humid conditions expected in western Sarawak this week could potentially reduce the impact of transboundary haze.
ASMC said satellite imagery from the United States National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration helped to detect hotspots.
However, those could go undetected due to cloudy conditions or during gaps in satellite coverage, it added.
Meanwhile, Hisham said air quality could improve with the change in wind direction due to the onset of the northeast monsoon.

The hearing was nominally on the international finance system, including reforms to the International Monetary Fund and World Bank, but lawmakers peppered Bessent with questions about more pressing issues, such as the state of financial markets and the economy, and the administration's financial measures against Iran.

As the hearing got under way, several protesters stood up one after another to call for an end to sanctions on Iran and the war, forcing Bessent to stop and restart his opening statement. The people were hustled from the room.

Bessent told reporters rising bond yields were due to "global issues," as he headed into the hearing. The US 10-year Treasury yield hit peaks on Tuesday not seen since 2007 amid a global bond rout experienced by most other large economies.

Analysts tie the US bond yield increase to higher oil prices and expectations the Federal Reserve will raise its policy rate this week, as well as competition for capital from AI spending and concerns about the US fiscal trajectory.
During the hearing, Bessent acknowledged the rise in the 10-year yield reflects "the need to address the deficit," among other factors.

US bond yields have risen despite the Treasury's decision to double the size of longer-term debt buybacks that Bessent has described as a way to inject liquidity and counter the rise in yields, or at least slow it down.
Bessent told lawmakers the buybacks were successful in keeping yields from rising more, and that they underscored US credibility.

"There is a counterfactual of what would it have done — and we then proceeded to have the two most successful Treasury auctions that we've had in 20 years," Bessent told the congressional hearing. "Since President Trump has come in, (the US bond market) has been the best-performing bond market in the developed world."

He also defended the Treasury's joint intervention with Japan to shore up its currency, saying the US purchased a "nominal amount" of yen to signal support for Japanese policies, and made tens of millions of dollars in the process.
"A stronger yen is better for American exports. A stronger yen means that the Japanese government will not have to sell US assets to finance foreign currency intervention," Bessent added.
BESSENT HIGHLIGHTS FALLING POVERTY RATE

Several Democratic lawmakers pressed Bessent on the state of the economy, inflation and the rising cost of living — tying it to the Iran war and the run-up in global oil prices. Bessent blamed inflation on the previous Biden administration, and said Americans are better off under Trump.

He pointed to fresh data from the US Census Bureau showing that the percentage of Americans in poverty last year dipped 0.5 percentage point to the lowest rate on record, 10.2 per cent, with 34.5 million Americans in poverty. Median household income increased 2.6 per cent last year to a record US$87,460.

Bessent was also asked if Trump's proposal to pay each American US$5,000 if the Republican Party maintains congressional majorities in the November elections was serious. He said he would work with House Speaker Mike Johnson to make those payments happen if congressional approval proved necessary.
Bessent said the US dollar's strength reflects the Trump administration's credibility.

"A strong dollar is not a price on a screen; it is a set of behaviours, and what we have seen in this administration, where we are creating regulatory certainty, tax certainty, trade certainty and energy certainty that is bringing in trillions of dollars into the US," Bessent said.
AI SAFETY CONCERNS

Democrats questioned Bessent on concerns over increasingly powerful AI models after Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called on AI companies to slow the rate of advancement to ensure their safety — sentiments echoed by OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Elon Musk, who runs xAI.

Asked about the administration's position on this, Bessent said the Treasury has "been working on safety nonstop since the release of Mythos" earlier this year, working with banks to share patches for cybersecurity software vulnerabilities exposed by the Anthropic model.

He said the administration forced Anthropic to withdraw a model for safety checks, and that AI labs should be held accountable for their creations, but it was important to stay ahead of China in the AI development race.

"I can tell you what we shouldn't do on safety is to give these labs a liability exemption, which is what they are asking for," Bessent said. "The best way to guarantee safety is that the creators are liable for what they build and generate, and put out into the economy and to the American people and to the world populace."

3a5c14089eb77dd6: LA GUAIRA: Schools in Venezuela's quake-scarred coastal state of La Guaira were deserted on Tuesday, a day after the start of the new school year, with many parents opting to keep children home for fear of further deadly tremors.
La Guaira, home to a popular resort of the same name north of Venezuela's capital Caracas, was devastated by powerful back-to-back quakes on June 24 that left over 6,500 people dead.
Dozens of schools were damaged in the worst disaster in the Caribbean country in decades, which reduced hundreds of buildings to rubble.
A further 60 schools were converted into shelters for thousands of people left homeless by the magnitude 7.2 and 7.5 quakes.
In some areas, lessons are being taught under a tarp.
In one such tented school on Tuesday, a teacher drew a circle on a blackboard as part of a discussion with 14 students on managing their emotions.

"They're still very sensitive. In any conversation you have with them, they always bring it (the earthquake) up, and it's always good to listen to them so they can process all that pent-up emotion," María Herrera, the 43-year-old teacher, explained to AFP.
Many parents were too fearful of a repeat disaster to allow their children back into a bricks-and-mortar classroom.
Just over 300 students have enrolled for the new school year at John Paul II Diocesan Educational Unit, one of the few schools open in the port city of La Guaira.
The school has capacity for more than double that.
Only seven children showed up on Tuesday.
"The return to classes will be gradual and safe, focusing primarily on the emotional well-being not only of our students but also of our staff," said the principal, Marco Antonio Espinoza.
Yanet Dominguez, a fifth-grade teacher at the school, said parents had been plying her with questions about the building's structural safety.
"I told them yes, that improvements have been made to the building this year, and that they shouldn't be afraid to send their children," she said.
Amni Nunez, a 40-year-old industrial engineer, sent his two young children back to school after deciding that life must go on.
"They need to understand that the world keeps spinning and that we have to learn to live with this new reality," he told AFP.

KUALA LUMPUR: The use of artificial intelligence (AI) in Malaysia's healthcare sector could gain traction, driven by its low cost, ease of access and ability to provide personalised responses to patients.

Hong Leong Investment Bank Bhd (HLIB Research) cited a Boston Consulting Group (BCG) survey showing that a majority of adults polled across 15 countries in November 2025 had already used generative AI tools for health-related issues.
It added that an OpenAI survey in December 2025 found that three in five adults in the United States had used AI tools for health-related questions in the preceding three months.

"While there is currently limited data on Malaysians' use of large language models (LLMs) for healthcare-related queries, we take reference from the other regions as an indication of the potential trend in Malaysia," HLIB Research said in a note.
According to the BCG survey, higher-income individuals were substantially more likely to use LLMs for healthcare-related purposes.
The firm said the use of LLMs as a first point of consultation could have meaningful implications for hospital demand, particularly by breaking the "wait and see" mentality among patients.

HLIB Research said LLMs allow patients to better understand the potential significance of their symptoms and determine appropriate next steps, which could prompt them to seek professional care earlier and increase demand for healthcare services.
It said the potential was particularly relevant in Malaysia, where many health conditions remain under-diagnosed.

HLIB Research said the growing use of LLMs for healthcare queries could provide a more immediate tailwind for Malaysian hospital operators, such as IHH Healthcare Bhd, Sunway Healthcare Holdings Bhd and KPJ Healthcare Bhd.
Its top picks are IHH, with a target price of RM9.10, and KPJ, with a target price of RM3.79.
The firm maintained its "neutral" call on the healthcare sector.
e009fde4cd830e7b: NASA's Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope is gliding toward its distant observation post on a pinpoint trajectory so precise that engineers estimate the spacecraft's fuel load will last twice as long as their initial expectations, the space agency confirmed Monday.

The $4.3 billion observatory's designers originally planned to load enough propellant into Roman's four fuel tanks for a minimum lifetime of five years, plus a potential five-year mission extension. That was a conservative estimate. NASA officials knew an on-target launch and perfect execution of the observatory's first post-launch course correction maneuver would leave Roman with a hearty fuel reserve.

5bc8a415d867f489: IPSWICH: Mikel Arteta hailed the "unbelievable" Max Dowman after Arsenal's teenage sensation inspired their 4-2 win against Ipswich in the League Cup on Tuesday.

He has since completed his GCSE exams and is looking forward to a bright future with Arsenal.
Dowman's potential is obvious but becoming a key player for Arsenal won't be easy.
Many teenage stars have flamed out before reaching their potential and Arteta is determined to be a nurturing presence for the youngster.
"He is 16, we don't really see that in the Premier League," Arteta said.
"In this environment, we want to develop him and we need to look after him."
With Dowman waiting in the wings, Arsenal will return to action at Brighton on Saturday in their last game before the international break.
Arteta's team have won all six of their matches this season across the Premier League, Champions League and League Cup.
Having made a host of changes against Ipswich, Arteta was impressed with the desire of his understudies.
"That's what we want to, to face every game, every competition with the same mentality, attitude and desire and so far we are doing it," he said.

c1b59c620e550ad0: THE HAGUE: Former Philippines president Rodrigo Duterte is expected to appear in public for the first time on Wednesday since being transferred to the International Criminal Court 18 months ago to face murder charges related to his war on drugs.

Duterte, 81, served as president from 2016 to 2022, before being charged with crimes against humanity for creating, funding and arming death squads that targeted narcotics peddlers and users. He was arrested and taken to The Hague in March 2025.

On Wednesday, judges will hear arguments about his health and ability to stand trial, which is scheduled to begin in November. His lawyers have argued that he suffers from cognitive decline and is not well enough.
Duterte's lawyer and family did not respond to requests for comment.
ICC judges said in January that Duterte's health was good enough for him to follow proceedings and requested his presence in court, rather than by video link from the detention unit.

Duterte's warrant says he was responsible for a widespread and systematic campaign that led to thousands of killings between 2011 and 2019, including when he served as mayor of the southern Davao city.
ICC prosecutors have said as many as 30,000 people may have been killed in the crackdown, the details of which were reported in a Reuters investigation.

According to police, 6,200 suspects were killed during anti-drug operations. Duterte said he instructed police to act in self-defence and told supporters he was ready to "rot in jail" if it meant ridding the Philippines of illicit drugs.
488ddb1c2bc3769c: ELCHE: Real Madrid substitute Carlos Espi snatched his team a last-gasp 3-2 win at Elche on Tuesday to pull them level with Barcelona at the top of La Liga.
The striker, who already saved his team at Espanyol in their opening game with a late strike, tucked home at the back post in the 91st minute after Madrid threw away a two-goal lead.
Espi, who Madrid signed this summer from Levante, has not started a game for the club but both of his goals have been vital for Jose Mourinho's side.
Madrid have five wins from six matches, level on points with champions Barca, who host Racing Santander on Wednesday.
"(Espi) comes on with great motivation, (but) he has in front of him a player who is not a normal player," said Mourinho of Kylian Mbappe, who also scored for Madrid.
"Playing with the two of them is not easy... with the changes I made late on I risked everything, because a draw was not enough."
Mourinho was unhappy with his team not extending their 2-0 lead and allowing Elche, now bottom of La Liga, to fight back.
"There are games which seem to be over... which we're not killing off, and after not killing them off they go from easy to being out of control," added the veteran coach.
Mourinho rested Jude Bellingham for the first time this season, bringing Arda Guler into the team in his place.

Players from both teams wore t-shirts in support of residents from the city of Ceuta after the recent migration crisis in the Spanish territory in north Africa, although Mbappe, Vinicius Junior and Ibrahima Konate rolled them halfway up, appearing to slightly obscure the message "we are all Ceutans."
Vinicius has been struggling for his best form this season and missed some presentable opportunities at the Martinez Valero stadium.
The forward prodded wide after Guler set him up in the second minute, and he also sent another effort badly off-target from the edge of the box.
Tete Morente threatened at the other end but Madrid were on top and took the lead midway through the first half.
Guler curled a free-kick around the wall and against the post, with the ball hitting Elche goalkeeper Matias Dituro before it crossed the line, for an own goal.
Madrid's second came eight minutes later, created by record signing Yan Diomande, who registered his first assist for the club.
Starting for the second time, the Ivorian winger crossed for Mbappe to slip past Dituro for his eighth goal of the season across all competitions.
Mbappe collided with the goalkeeper and appeared to be hurt but soon recovered and was able to play on.
The striker combined again with Diomande early in the second half but could only head the winger's blasted cross high over the bar.
Vinicius drilled wide before he was replaced, ending a frustrating evening for the Brazil international.
Elche battle back
Elche pulled one back through Abiel Osorio's header from Lucas Cepeda's cross, with the forward leaping high to nod past Thibaut Courtois.
It struck fear into Los Blancos and Elche capitalised, equalising in the 83rd minute through Nino.
The Spanish striker produced a fine low finish to pull his team level with the 15-time European champions.
Mourinho threw on strikers Espi and Endrick to try and find a late winner, and he got what he was looking for.
Espi made a run to the back post where Mbappe found him to knock in the late winner.
Earlier Valencia earned a 1-0 win at Alaves, while Rayo Vallecano defeated Espanyol 2-1.
It was Valencia's first win of the season, after they sacked coach Carlos Corberan on Sunday, secured with a Luis Rioja strike with 12 minutes to go.

MORE than 2.7 billion people, including 767 million children aged up to 14, were exposed to second-hand smoke globally in 2023, according to a study published in 'The Lancet'.
This exposure contributed to nearly 1.7 million premature deaths and extensive illness, led by ischemic heart disease, while causing 5.2 million respiratory tract infections in children.
Tobacco remains a leading cause of disease globally, with non-smokers making up a notable portion of the estimated eight million smoking-related deaths in 2023.
"Exposure to second-hand smoke is a globally recognised health risk, with no safe level of inhalation," it said.

Analysing data from 204 countries and territories between 1990 and 2023, researchers explained that non-smokers near active smokers inhale both exhaled smoke and sidestream smoke from the burning tobacco.

"The sidestream component, which dominates the air non-smokers breathe, is unfiltered, carrying higher per-unit concentrations of the toxic and carcinogenic compounds than the smoke inhaled by active smokers," it said.
Despite drops in overall smoking prevalence since 1990, the total number of people exposed has stayed stable due to population growth and rising exposure in Africa and the Middle East.
Women are disproportionately affected, especially in regions where female smoking rates are low.
"Despite this substantial burden, (second-hand smoke) exposure remains rarely acknowledged as a major risk factor for female health."
To safeguard vulnerable groups, the study urged governments to enforce stricter tobacco controls across public places and homes to better protect women and children. — AFP
b71465a36e78b6c1: LOS ANGELES: The artist Finneas and three other supporting acts announced they had quit British superstar Ed Sheeran's tour on Tuesday, after rapper Macklemore was dropped for making pro-Palestinian comments while performing.
Sheeran has denied being behind the decision to remove Macklemore, saying his tour's promoter was responsible.

But Finneas – a performer also famous for work with his superstar sister Billie Eilish – Irish acts Aaron Rowe and Beoga, and Lukas Graham of Denmark all posted they were quitting Sheeran's "Loop Tour."
While opening for Sheeran earlier this month at New Jersey's MetLife Stadium, Macklemore shouted "Free Palestine!" and told Palestinians they were "not forgotten."

"Macklemore coming off tour was the promoter's decision, it was not mine," Sheeran wrote in a lengthy Instagram post, adding that the rapper's contract was ended by the promoter, Messina Touring Group.
According to Sheeran, venues on the tour "communicated that they would pull the shows if he was still supporting."

The artist said he held prolonged discussions with venue managers, including Robert Kraft, owner of Boston's Gillette Stadium and the Patriots NFL team. But he was unable to resolve the issue, he added.
Finneas has publicly advocated for Palestinians in the past. He posted Tuesday that "artists must not be silenced when they speak up for the oppressed."
"I stand with Palestine and its people."
Sheeran's touring band Beoga said they were dropping out "following the silencing of Macklemore by Zionist lobbies."

"We are a traditional Irish band who never saw ourselves playing in stadiums of that size and that opportunity is not lost on us," the group said, adding they had been friends with Sheeran for a decade and would stay so.
But "we are Irish people who understand colonialism," Beoga said on Instagram.
"As founding members of the Irish Artists for Palestine movement, we are committed activists for justice and will continue to be."
Irish artist Rowe similarly cited his country's history in explaining the decision to drop out.
"As Irish people we know all too well about genocide, forced famine and violent occupation," he wrote, also noting that Sheeran was a friend who "has changed my life."
Yet "I cannot stand by and allow billionaires to use their position of power to silence the rightful voices of those who speak up against Israeli genocide," Rowe said.
'Strength of purpose'
In his post Tuesday, Sheeran had touched on his decision not to comment publicly about political subjects, notably the war in Gaza.
"I am not complicit. I have my personal views on this devastating conflict. Just because I choose not to speak publicly, it doesn't mean I don't care," he said.
"Those who come to my shows do not expect a political forum. I respect Macklemore's strength of purpose."
On Monday, Macklemore posted that Sheeran and his team were not behind his departure from the tour.
He said that Kraft had contacted Sheeran to tell him the rapper would not be allowed on stage and alleged that Kraft had rallied other venues to demand his exclusion.
In a statement, Kraft said that Gillette Stadium would "not provide a platform for hate speech."
Macklemore, known for hits including "Thrift Shop" and "Can't Hold Us," has long vocally supported Palestinians.
In 2024 he released "Hind's Hall," which pays tribute to Hind Rajab, a five-year-old Palestinian girl whose death sparked a wave of international outrage.

be2350ad29ca3d8c: LONDON: Liverpool piled on the misery for troubled Tottenham with a 3-1 win in the League Cup third round, while teenage star Max Dowman dazzled for Arsenal in their 4-2 rout of Ipswich on Tuesday.
After a woeful start to the Premier League season, Tottenham's hopes of a morale-boosting cup run came to a dispiriting end at rain-lashed Anfield.
They were swatted aside by Liverpool, with Alexis Mac Allister, Cody Gakpo and Dominik Szoboszlai scoring for the Reds.
Roberto De Zerbi's fourth-bottom team are without a win or even a goal in their first four league matches, losing twice and drawing twice.
Tottenham's only win this season has come in the League Cup against second-tier Charlton.

After successive 17th place finishes -- including avoiding relegation on the final day of last season -- the north London club spent over £300 million (US$404 million) on 10 new signings since the end of last term.
But the return on that eye-watering investment has not been immediate, sparking fears of another relegation battle.
Adding to De Zerbi's problems, unsettled striker Richarlison took to social media to lament the Italian's decision to leave him out of the squad to face Liverpool.
Richarlison wants to leave but moves to Everton and Vasco Da Gama have fallen through recently.
Tottenham host Aston Villa on Saturday in a game that De Zerbi desperately needs to win to ease the pressure on him going into the international break.
Liverpool remain unbeaten at the start of the Andoni Iraola era, although they have won just once in four league matches.
Iraola made 10 changes but Liverpool went ahead after 21 minutes with a flowing move.
Gakpo picked out Rio Ngumoha and he teed up Mac Allister to blast a first-time finish past Martin Dubravka into the roof of the net.
Gakpo doubled Liverpool's advantage in the 54th minute, whipping a fine strike into the far corner.
Tottenham finally scored a goal against top-flight opposition this season -- albeit in a different competition -- when Conor Gallagher punished poor marking to net from a corner in the 69th minute.
But Szoboszlai rubbed salt into Tottenham's wounds in stoppage-time with a 25-yard rocket.
At Portman Road, Dowman took centre stage to remember Arsenal manager Mikel Arteta of his burgeoning talent.
Arsenal, who lost the League Cup final against Manchester City last season, have won their six games in all competitions this term.
Arteta made nine changes from the side that won at Sunderland on Saturday, with 16-year-old Dowman given his first appearance this season.
Dowman has been ear-marked as a future star since bursting onto the scene as a 15-year-old last season.
But Arteta is treating the midfielder with kid gloves, bringing him on slowly while the Premier League champions are thriving.
Dowman showed Arteta what he can add to the party in the seventh minute, flashing quick feet to skip past Cedric Kipre before slotting home with a composed finish.
It was Dowman's second goal for Arsenal after his strike against Everton in March.
Noni Madueke increased Arsenal's lead in the 16th minute, lashing a low shot past Christian Walton from just inside the penalty area.
Dowman struck again in the 47th minute, running onto Martin Zubimendi's pass and finishing with aplomb.
Mikel Merino grabbed Arsenal's fourth, curling home from Dowman's pass in the 58th minute.
Anis Mehmeti's 62nd minute reply and Chuba Akpom's stoppage-time strike were little consolation for out-classed Ipswich.
Fulham made nine changes but still won 3-2 at Championship leaders West Ham, with goals from Rodrigo Muniz, Cesar Palacios and Oscar Bobb, who bagged the 78th minute winner.
Brentford won 2-1 at third tier Reading thanks to goals from Callum Wilson and Fabio Carvalho.
On Wednesday, Manchester United host Brighton, Aston Villa travel to Coventry and Everton face Wolves.
Holders Manchester City are at home to Norwich on Thursday.

0ebe44525223390a: NEW YORK: Wall Street extended its selloff on Tuesday, as rising US Treasury yields, mounting debt concerns and soaring crude prices kept buyers on the sidelines.

All three major US stock indexes extended Monday's losses as broad risk-off sentiment weighed on nearly every sector but energy. That sector benefited from expanding hostilities in the Middle East, which included new attacks on Saudi Arabia's energy infrastructure.

"Given rising prices for fuel, especially diesel, given the near-certain outlook for rising rates beginning tomorrow, and given the concerns over the potential slowdown in the AI ecosphere, why step into the market aggressively until some of this clears up?" said Peter Tuz, president of Chase Investment Counsel in Charlottesville, Virginia.

The Federal Reserve has convened for its two-day monetary policy meeting, which is due to culminate on Wednesday with the central bank's rate decision. With recent economic data showing the labour market on solid footing, while war-related energy price pressures are morphing into broader, systemic inflation, the central bank is expected to implement a 25-basis-point increase to its Fed funds target rate — its first interest rate hike in over three years.

In the wake of last week's hot inflation data and the near 25% jump in US crude pricesCLc1 over the last two weeks, financial markets have priced in a 94.5% likelihood of a rate hike on Wednesday, up from 33.1% one month ago, according to CME's FedWatch tool.
Tuz added that while markets will learn the Fed's decision tomorrow, "the Middle East conflict is a wild card as to how long it might last."
Front-month West Texas Intermediate and Brent oil settled up 4.4% and 2.9% respectively, while diesel futures HOc1 closed at a record high.

"This will probably be not a one-and-done, but a series of rate increases," said Paul Nolte, senior wealth adviser and market strategist at Murphy & Sylvest in Elmhurst, Illinois. "It will be dependent on oil; that is really the source of inflation and it's starting to seep into other parts of the market."
As rate-hike bets increased, global bond yields resumed their upward climb, with benchmark US Treasury yields breaching 5% and reaching the highest level since 2007.
Rising interest rates are increasing the pressure on heavily indebted borrowers, including companies that have placed big bets on AI.

Those worries exacerbated mounting fears over AI's destructive potential and growing opposition to the construction of data centers, which came to a head on Monday and dragged the Philadelphia SE Semiconductor index.
The semiconductor index, which has helped drive broader stock market gains this year, did not meaningfully recover from Monday's rout, eking out a 0.4% gain.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 328.09 points, or 0.63%, to 52,093.11, the S&P 500 lost 34.25 points, or 0.45%, to 7,585.73 and the Nasdaq Composite lost 204.84 points, or 0.78%, to 25,981.57.

b68cf4dd77f138dd: GENEVA: The World Food Programme said Tuesday that it would have to end food aid to two million people in South Sudan in the weeks because of a lack of funds.
About 7.8 million people, about half of the African country's population, struggle to get enough food each day, according to the UN agency's assistant executive director Matthew Hollingworth.

The WFP gives daily support to about three million of them and the number would fall to one million by the end of the month unless it receives "a very significant uptick in resources very soon", Hollingworth told reporters.
He estimated that US$86 million was needed immediately and US$416 million over the next six months to keep up the assistance.
Some 2.2 million children and 1.2 million pregnant and breastfeeding women require "urgent nutrition support", said Hollingworth.
"Unless additional resources are secured, more than a million vulnerable people could lose access to life-saving food and nutrition assistance by October."
The agency's shrinking resources were already visible on the ground. Hollingworth said WFP warehouses in Malakal held 10,000 tonnes of food a year ago but now contain fewer than 300 tonnes.
Since its independence in 2011, South Sudan has been hit by a series of internal conflicts. It has also taken in more than one million refugees from the civil war in neighbouring Sudan.
Economic difficulties and climate-related pressures have further worsened the humanitarian situation.
"We are about to drop off a financial cliff at a time when the needs are at the greatest level that they've been at for the past 13, 14 years," Hollingworth said.

1a87ed2fc5be82b2: WASHINGTON: The six-month-old US war against Iran has cost US$38 billion so far and that amount is projected to rise by US$3 billion a month, Congress' nonpartisan bookkeeper reported on Tuesday, as the Trump administration searches for ways to end the conflict and reopen the vital Strait of Hormuz.
The war is expected to increase inflation by 0.5% in the first three months of 2027, according to the Congressional Budget Office (CBO) accounting, which totalled expenses through Aug 1.

The mounting costs have strained US munitions stockpiles and driven up energy prices, raising concerns about the country's ability to respond to other potential conflicts and adding pressure on an already stretched federal budget.
The cost was close to the US$37.5 billion that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth reported at a Senate hearing on July 21.

The budget office said the majority of the costs stem from the rapid drawdown of munitions, estimating that it could take five years to replenish US stockpiles. Reuters reported in August that the US had used "virtually all" of its long-range precision missiles during the war.
The Department of Defense did not cooperate with congressional financial auditors, CBO reported.
Representatives from the White House and Department of Defense did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
The inquiry was conducted at the request of the top Democrat on the US House of Representatives Budget Committee, Brendan Boyle of Pennsylvania.
“Donald Trump’s disastrous war in Iran has already taken the lives of brave American servicemembers and left others wounded," Boyle said in a statement.
"Beyond that human toll, this nonpartisan CBO report makes clear that the war has also cost American taxpayers tens of billions of dollars and counting, while continuing to drive up costs."
Eighteen US military service members have died in the Iran war.

The report did not include costs of recent strikes on commercial vessels in the Strait of Hormuz and attacks on US military installations in the region. It also did not factor in the borrowing expenses associated with financing the war, which could add tens of billions of dollars to the total cost.
The CBO accounting found the war could have sprawling consequences for the US defense posture and the domestic economy.

The deficit in critical munitions, including missile interceptors, risks hampering the Pentagon's response in the event of another major conflict, such as potential hostilities involving China and Taiwan, CBO said.
At the July hearing in the Senate, Hegseth pleaded for nearly US$90 billion emergency funding legislation to restock munitions supplies.
“Without these funds, we face critical shortfalls,” Hegseth said.

Energy shocks caused by attacks in the Strait of Hormuz — the narrow waterway through which roughly 20% of the world's oil traveled before the war — and on energy facilities in neighboring Gulf countries have sharply increased prices for consumers and global producers.
The rising cost of the war also threatens to weigh on deteriorating US fiscal health. The nation's total public debt surpassed US$40 trillion in August.
Trump regularly contrasts the Iran war with the US invasions of Iraq and Afghanistan that followed the Sept 11, 2001, attacks.

The eight-year US war in Iraq, which involved more than 100,000 ground troops at its peak, cost US$2 trillion, Reuters reported. The two-decade-long US conflict in Afghanistan, which also involved more than 100,000 troops at its most intense, cost US$2.3 trillion, according to Brown University's Costs of War project.
3155826eac69a632: TORONTO: Prime Minister Mark Carney pitched Canada as an investment haven Tuesday at a gathering of global financial elite, but conceded ties with the United States remained crucial despite an escalating trade war.
Carney convened the Canada Investment Summit as part of his push to diversify an economy he insists had grown too reliant on an increasingly protectionist US.

The guest list for the event in Toronto included representatives of Gulf investment agencies and major European banks, as well as Africa's richest man, Nigerian tycoon Aliko Dangote, along with US investors.

"Our goal is to catalyze CAN$1 trillion (US$720 billion) of investment in Canada over the next five years," Carney told the event, promising tax incentives and reduced bureaucracy to make the country more attractive to foreign capital.
Carney said Canada had the reserves of critical minerals and clean energy that the world needs, calling these sectors the keys to "strategic autonomy."
He particularly highlighted plans to build a new pipeline to the Pacific coast "that would carry at least one million barrels of low-emission Alberta oil per day to Asian markets."
"We are unleashing our full potential as an energy superpower," the prime minister said.
But in his opening address, hours after Trump imposed new tariffs on certain Canadian goods, Carney offered an optimistic view of future relations with the United States.
"To our American friends, let me say this: We will always be neighbours, and Canada will continue to be the US's most important partner in many key areas," he said.
He said the two countries had always maintained close ties, "even at times of disagreement."
"These arrangements work when we engage as true partners that respect each other's traditions and sovereignty," Carney told attendees at a luxury hotel in central Toronto.
"When those opportunities return, Canada will be an even better partner, stronger, more resilient, more independent," he said.

The Canadian leader, a former investment banker who previously led the central banks of Canada and England, also revived themes he articulated in a high-profile address to the World Economic Forum in January -- a speech that drew a direct rebuke from Trump.

"Sovereignty and openness are now in tension. Economic integration is being weaponized. Tariffs are used as leverage," he said on Tuesday, adding that supply chains are now used as "vulnerabilities to be exploited."

Speaking to reporters after his address, Carney was asked about his conciliatory tone toward the US after saying last month that any deal signed with the US would be written in "pencil," deriding the trustworthiness of the Trump administration.
Carney said he continues to believe that a "mutually beneficial trade deal is possible" with Washington. "Canada continues to stand ready to develop that and pursue it," he said.
Later Tuesday, Carney was to fly to Strasbourg, France, where he will become the first head of government to attend the State of the European Union address.
Closer ties with the EU are at the core of Canada's strategy to pivot away from reliance on the US.
Carney has said he is seeking a "unique alliance" with the bloc and was pressed Tuesday for details on what that might include.
He said Canada and the EU intend to hammer out their future relationship at a summit next month in Montreal.
It's crucial for Canada to be "connected to partners on which we can rely," Carney said.
